articles.title: US to lay fresh torture charges against Venezuela's Maduro and wife
articles.summary: Prosecutors are considering charges over the alleged torture of more than a dozen Americans detained in Venezuela. Meanwhile, Cilia Flores is seeking release from jail on health grounds.

image.caption: Maduro and Flores both already face drug trafficking and firearms charges in the US [FILE: January 5, 2026]Image: Adam Gray/REUTERS

blocks.text: US prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans held in Venezuela, a US official said late on Wednesday.
The charges could be announced as soon as Thursday and reportedly concern the alleged wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens during Maduro's 13-year rule.
Prosecutors are also considering charges against others allegedly involved in the torture.
Details of the potential new charges and the alleged victims were not immediately available.
Maduro's wife seeks release
Meanwhile, the 69-year-old Flores is due in Manhattan federal court on Thursday where she is expected to ask a judge to release her from jail and place her under house arrest, citing health problems.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds in custody, suffers from dizziness and shortness of breath and may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
They have proposed that she live at a New York residence under 24-hour security.

blocks.caption: Media reports said prosecutors are also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing Americans [FILE: March 26, 2026]Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

blocks.text: Prosecutors, however, oppose the request, arguing that Flores poses an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released.
They said she has received hospital treatment when necessary, while in custody.
Trump vs Maduro
Maduro, 63, and Flores are being held at a federal detention center in Brooklyn as they await their trial in June next year.
The couple was captured during an unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid on their Caracas home on January 3, which was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation."
Critics have accused Trump of operating outside international law.
They were subsequently brought to New York, where they face existing drug trafficking and firearms charges.
Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Meanwhile, in August, Trump announced that the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, which Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez also termed "historic."

articles.title: More threat data is useful only if security teams can act on it
articles.summary: Security teams have access to more threat intelligence than ever, but the volume of information can create another problem: figuring out what actually needs attention. Security Operations Centers are…

blocks.text: Security teams have access to more threat intelligence than ever, but the volume of information can create another problem: figuring out what actually needs attention.

Security Operations Centers are already handling large numbers of alerts every day, often with fewer people than they need. Attackers are also moving quickly, leaving analysts less time to determine which indicators point to an active threat and which can be deprioritized.

This puts a practical limit on the value of threat intelligence. An organization may have extensive information about malicious activity, but analysts still need to sort through that information before they can act on it.

Kaspersky is adding new AI capabilities to its Threat Intelligence Portal to address that problem. The features include AI-generated summaries of human-readable threat intelligence and support for the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, which allows third-party AI applications to connect to the portal.
Making threat intelligence easier to review
During an investigation or threat-hunting exercise, analysts can encounter hundreds of Indicators of Compromise (IoCs), along with reports covering threat actors, campaigns, and related activity.

Kaspersky’s new summarization feature condenses information associated with an indicator into a shorter overview. The aim is to give analysts enough context to decide whether an IoC warrants a closer look without requiring them to immediately work through every available source.
The company says the summaries are generated from selected source datasets, allowing analysts to see the context behind the information rather than receiving an isolated AI-generated answer.

The feature can also be used with IoCs discovered through open-source intelligence searches. Analysts can use the AI-generated summaries to get an initial view of the information associated with an entity and determine where a deeper investigation is needed.

This does not replace the analyst’s role in evaluating the intelligence. It changes the first stage of the process. Analysts can use the summary to narrow their focus, then examine the underlying information when an indicator or threat actor requires further investigation.

That can be particularly useful for teams dealing with large volumes of intelligence, as well as less-experienced analysts who may otherwise have to work through extensive information before establishing where to begin.
Connecting threat intelligence to AI applications
Kaspersky is also introducing MCP connectivity, allowing organizations to connect their own AI applications or third-party AI tools to the Threat Intelligence Portal.

MCP provides a way for AI applications to interact with external tools and data sources. For threat intelligence, that means an AI application can query information from Kaspersky’s portal when it needs it, rather than requiring analysts to manually move information between separate systems.
Instead of limiting AI to tasks such as summarizing reports, organizations can connect it to external sources that allow it to retrieve information as part of a larger workflow.

Kaspersky says its threat intelligence is built on more than 25 petabytes of proprietary threat context. That amount of data can provide security teams with a broad view of malicious activity, but it also illustrates the problem that AI is being used to address. The more intelligence available to analysts, the more difficult it can become to review everything manually.

For security teams dealing with high alert volumes and staffing constraints, the value of AI may therefore be less about producing more intelligence and more about making existing intelligence easier to work with.
Kaspersky’s new features are aimed at reducing the time between finding a piece of threat intelligence and determining what it means for an organization’s security operation.

articles.summary: Mark Villar’s move comes as the Office of the Ombudsman announced graft complaints against his family over PrimeWater contracts, and amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte before…

blocks.text: VILLARS. Senators Mark and Camille Villar during a Senate session on July 29, 2025.
Senate Social Media Unit

Mark Villar’s move comes as the Office of the Ombudsman announced graft complaints against his family over PrimeWater contracts, and amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte before senator-judges
MANILA, Philippines — Senator Mark Villar has joined the Senate majority bloc, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III confirmed Thursday, October 8.
“Well, apparently,” Sotto told reporters in an ambush interview when asked about Villar’s transfer.
“We’re glad because we’re all loaded with work… We have the impeachment, legislative [duties], and budget [deliberations], so it would be better if we have more members,” he said.
Sotto said he was informed of the change only earlier in the day and that Senate Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri coordinated Villar’s transfer.
The Senate held its final plenary session on Thursday before going on a break from October 9 to November 9.

During the session, Zubiri moved for the election of Villar as a member of the Commission on Appointments (CA) under the majority bloc. Villar was also elected chairperson of the Senate committee on public works and highways, replacing Sotto.
Asked if Villar had formally joined the majority, Zubiri said: “Yes, we just elected him to the CA and public works committee as part of the majority.”
With Villar’s transfer, the majority bloc now has 14 members, while the minority has 10. His sister, Senator Camille Villar, remains with the minority bloc.

Villar’s move came as the Office of the Ombudsman announced graft complaints against members of the Villar family over contracts involving their firm, PrimeWater. It also comes amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, which will be decided by senator-judges. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Supreme Court eases process for recognizing foreign divorces in Philippines
articles.summary: In the high court’s En Banc session on October 7, the Court said the new rules eliminate the requirement that petitioners independently prove the foreign divorce law in court, requiring them…

blocks.text: This file photo shows the seal of the Supreme Court.
Philstar.com / EC Toledo

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has approved amendments to the Rules of Court that streamline the legal process for Filipino spouses seeking Philippine judicial recognition of foreign divorces.

In the high court’s En Banc session on October 7, the Court said the new rules eliminate the requirement that petitioners independently prove the foreign divorce law in court, requiring them only to establish that the divorce decree was issued.

The newly introduced provision under Rule 39 establishes a legal presumption that a foreign divorce obtained between a Filipino and a foreign spouse is absolute and allows the foreign spouse to remarry under foreign law, unless the decree explicitly specifies that it is a limited divorce.
Under the amended rules, the burden of proof shifts to the opposing party to show that a foreign divorce is not absolute.

Furthermore, English translations of divorce documents are presumed accurate if certified under oath by the translator — a presumption that may be contested with contrary evidence, such as certified true copies of foreign divorce laws sourced from the Office of the Court Administrator's central repository.
“These presumptions are disputable, meaning they may be challenged with contrary evidence, under Section 3 of Rule 131,” the Supreme Court’s statement read.

“To challenge these presumptions, Section 24 of Rule 132 allows the submission of a certified true copy of the applicable foreign divorce law, including its English translation, obtained from the Office of the Court Administrator (OCA), which will maintain a repository of foreign laws,” it added.
However, the Supreme Court clarified that the core legal framework under Article 26(2) of the Family Code remains unchanged.
Filipino spouses must still file a formal petition for judicial recognition in Philippine courts.
Furthermore, petitions may still be opposed on established legal grounds, including lack of jurisdiction, lack of notice, fraud, or clear mistakes of law or fact.
Addressing challenges of OFWs

According to the High Court, it introduced these procedural changes after recognizing the significant hurdles Filipino spouses — especially Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) — face in proving foreign statutes.

Citing Department of Foreign Affairs findings, the high court noted that obtaining official certifications and English translations across varied international jurisdictions created unnecessary barriers, which these amendments seek to eliminate.

articles.summary: Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida on Thursday stressed that an alleged violation of the law is no small matter following Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste brushing off the issuance of an arrest…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 2:16pm

Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida on Thursday stressed that an alleged violation of the law is no small matter following Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste brushing off the issuance of an arrest warrant against him.

“Malaking pong bagay. Bakit po? Ang hindi pagsunod… sa batas ay malaking bagay. Itinakda ang batas para magkaroon po ng kaayusan, di ba? Kaya nagpapasa ang Kongreso. Kaya tayo nag-e-elect ng congressman at senador para ipasa to,” he said.

(It is a big deal. Why? Not following the law is a big deal. The law is established to maintain order, right? That is why Congress passes laws. That is why we elect congressmen and senators to pass them.)

On Wednesday, Leviste told his supporters not to worry about him after a Makati court issued the warrant for alleged violation of the Public Service Act, saying that this was “a small matter” compared to everything else.
Vida said that Leviste himself is a congressman, as is his mother, Senator Loren Legarda.
“Tayo ay sumusunod lamang doon sa mga batas na ipinasa nila dahil ang layunin nito ay magkaroon ng kaayusan,” he said.
(We are simply following the laws that they passed because the purpose of these laws is to maintain order.)
“Ang paggalang natin sa proseso ng Korte at ang paggalang natin sa korte at sa proseso nito, tulad ng arrest warrant, ay malaking bagay,” he added.
(Respecting the Court’s process and respecting the Court and its processes, such as an arrest warrant, is a big deal.)
The DOJ said it filed the case against Leviste and others on September 29 with the Makati Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 235.

“The position of the DOJ is that finding of prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction that the… Solar Corporation willfully neglected and intentionally failed to comply with its obligation,” it said. —AOL,GMA News

articles.title: Mark Villar reclaims public works chairship in switch to majority bloc
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Villar has regained chairship of the powerful Senate public works committee in his jump to the majority bloc.

blocks.text: Senator-judge Mark Villar attends Day 2 of the impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay City.
Mark Villar via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar has regained chairship of the powerful Senate public works committee in his jump to the majority bloc.

Majority Leader Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri confirmed Villar's switch to the majority during the plenary session Thursday, October 8, where he also announced Villar's election as chair of the public works panel, replacing Sen. Tito Sotto.
The Senate has also elected Villar as a member of the Commission on Appointments, replacing Zubiri.
The majority bloc now has 14 members.
Alongside the reshuffle, Minority Leader Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano was also elected as member of the Commission on Appointments, replacing Sen. Loren Legarda.
Mark's sister, Sen. Camille Villar, remains in the Cayetano-led minority bloc.
Mark previously broke with the minority bloc during the impeachment court's deliberations on whether to do away with the fixed 16-vote threshold for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte.
The senator had voted in favor of allowing the court to interpret with flexibility the Constitution's requirement of conviction by "two-thirds of all members" of the Senate.
Ombudsman probe
Both Villar siblings are facing an Ombudsman probe for alleged violations of the anti-graft law over joint ventures entered into by their former water utility firm PrimeWater Infrastructure Corp.

Besides the two sitting senators, the Ombudsman also named former Senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, businessman Manuel Paolo Villar, as well as PrimeWater executives Fe Reblancos and Romeo Sabater as respondents in the criminal and administrative complaints.
PrimeWater has been accused of entering into deals with local water districts between 2015 and 2022 that were skewed against the government's interest.
The agreements under scrutiny were signed during Mark's term as public works secretary and membership on the board of the Local Water Utilities Administration.

articles.title: University students say procrastination is biggest threat to their academic performance
articles.summary:
More than half of US students surveyed said the problem damaged their ability to do academic work, study finds

Procrastination is the biggest problem that can harm students’ academic…

blocks.text: Procrastination is the biggest problem that can harm students’ academic performance at university, according to a study of more than 65,000 young people who placed it above issues such as ADHD, anxiety or financial worries.

The study found that nearly half of the students surveyed named procrastination as the thing damaging their ability to do academic work, more than twice the number who named depression, while the same proportion said procrastination caused them significant distress above any other problems including family pressures or bullying.

Itamar Shatz, the author of the study and an affiliated lecturer at the University of Cambridge, said that while he expected the survey of US students would show that they experienced harm from procrastination, he was surprised by how strongly it affected them.

Shatz said: “Pretty much all of us procrastinate but it’s not a huge impediment for all of us. For the people that it is, it can be huge. It’s not just something we occasionally run into but, as we can see in these findings, it can be a major obstacle.

“It’s an obstacle that can interfere with academic success, with success in the workplace, it can cause issues in relationships, it can cause stress, it can cause health issues and stop us reaching out for help.”
The study, published in the journal Plos One, also suggests that procrastination could be a factor in a “vicious cycle” that can cause or exaggerate other issues such as stress.

“An example of such a feedback loop is a student procrastinating on a task, which causes them to feel stressed, which interferes with their sleep, which causes them to procrastinate on the task further,” the study said.

Fuschia Sirois, a psychology professor at Durham University and a co-editor-in-chief of the British Journal of Health Psychology, who was not involved in the study, said: “The salience of procrastination in students’ lives and its harms has been a topic of research for almost 30 years, with the first studies on the impact of procrastination on health and wellbeing conducted in the late 1990s and early 2000s. So this is an issue for which there is an established evidence base that clearly highlights the negative impact of procrastination on students’ lives.

“This descriptive study with a large sample provides some additional insights into the relative impact of procrastination with respect to its range of harms. But it is just a snapshot, so limits the conclusions we can draw.”
Sirois said myths about procrastination “being a character flaw” have persisted despite the existing research.

“People procrastinate to avoid the difficult emotions associated with a task, which affords them short-term mood repair. But in the long run the feelings of guilt, shame and stress from procrastinating catch up to them and take a toll on health and wellbeing,” she said.

Shatz, who has recently published a guide to overcoming procrastination, said that procrastination should not be compared with laziness, because procrastinators can often be highly motivated to tackle a task only to be derailed by other distractions such as perfectionism or burn-out.
Universities should be aware that many of their students are likely to be hampered by procrastination.

“They should understand that procrastination isn’t just a time management flaw that they can fix with a flyer, but it is one of the biggest obstacles that students face and needs to be treated with positive interventions. The good thing is that research shows that interventions can help,” Shatz said.

articles.title: Voting opens in high stakes Holborn and St Pancras byelection
articles.summary:
Zack Polanski has led energetic campaign for the Greens, while Labour will hope to hold on to Starmer’s old seat

Voting has opened in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as…

blocks.text: Voting has opened in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a key gauge of Andy Burnham’s ability to energise voters and whether Zack Polanski’s Greens can still peel off support from Labour’s left.

Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, is standing for his party in the north London constituency, previously held by Keir Starmer before he stood down as an MP shortly after resigning as prime minister.

The seat is, under normal circumstances, a Labour stronghold. Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Polanski. In 2019, Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes.

Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign. He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat.

However, the political landscape has changed. Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour.

Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies.

Polanski’s fortunes in contrast appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party.

blocks.caption: Zack Polanski has mobilised a large number of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection.  Photograph: Andy Hall/The Guardian

blocks.text: Four out of the five Green MPs have condemned the policy, while councillors and others have distanced themselves from it or in some cases left the party.

While policy is decided by Green members in direct votes, Polanski has been criticised for not saying whether or not he backed the motion and leaving the conference before the vote took place to resume campaigning.

The stakes are also high for Burnham. Failure to win the seat by a reasonable margin could end his honeymoon period and bring renewed doubts about Labour’s ability to protect inner-city seats from the Greens, who won several London councils in May’s local elections.
after newsletter promotion

Holborn and St Pancras could be promising ground for the Greens, with a young and diverse population that includes many students. About 45% of constituents were born overseas and 48% are aged between 18 and 34.

Labour has campaigned hard, fielding as its candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in London in the early 90s, speaking no English, after fleeing war in Somalia with her four brothers and her mother, who trained as a lawyer in Somalia.

In a pre-poll message to voters, Burnham said: “This area gave Sagal a home when she arrived here as a refugee in the 1990s. Camden gave Sagal and her family hope. Now she wants to give that back to the communities that have always been there for her. It’s hard to think of someone more committed to their local area and the care of people than Sagal.”
In his own statement, Polanski said the result was “looking close”, and that voters should choose him to pressure Labour.

He said: “We already have a Labour government, a Labour council and a Labour [London] mayor. Isn’t it time for a Green voice for Camden to push Labour to do better on issues like rent controls and to put Thames Water into public ownership – issues where they’ve been backtracking?”

articles.title: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Thinktank says Britain’s drive towards global commitments is symptom of ‘outdated foreign policy’

The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic…

blocks.text: The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned.

According to an analysis by researchers at the Transition Security Project, Britain has the most overseas-oriented military among European nations, with almost a quarter of the defence budget spent on commitments across five continents.

Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions which have often made the globe less safe, the report says the imminent uptick in spending should be accompanied by a change of stance, with a much bigger focus on domestic defence.
The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 amid a defence investment plan (Dip) unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership.
Starmer’s then defence secretary, John Healey, resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that he is chancellor that target has been shelved for now.

It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre which was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham.

Using figures from 2024/25, the study estimated that about 23% of the military budget for that year was spent on overseas commitments, costing just over £14bn, with the real figure likely to be higher. About £2.8bn was spent outside Europe, including bases in places like Cyprus, Kenya and Oman and elsewhere as “strategic hubs” for projecting UK military power.

The report says this makes the UK the most overseas-committed military among European Nato members, even if France has more personnel posted abroad. The Dip seems unlikely to reverse this, talking about ongoing commitments in a series of continents.
It questions whether more of the new money should be used for domestic defence, and whether the focus on overseas missions has even made the UK safer.
Since 2001, the study said, the UK has spent more than £51bn in modern terms on military interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya and elsewhere.

“Britain’s decision to maintain a global network of military bases and force projection capabilities, combined with high levels of waste in the military procurement system, raise serious questions about how it is allocating public investment,” it says, urging the government to “review its military posture, prioritising defence over the global projection of military force”.

Kevin Cashman, a researcher at Transition Security Project, who co-authored the report, said: “Britain should not pour more money into a bloated military sector geared towards alignment with the United States while Washington starts wars around the world that drive up our bills.”

Khem Rogaly, the co-director of the organisation, and also a co-author, said: “The billions of pounds Britain wastes on global military deployments every year symbolise its destructive, outdated foreign policy.

“Britain should end its support for these attempts at global policing. Instead, it should focus its military resources on defence and its public investment on health, housing and the climate emergency.”
There is an awareness of the importance of avoiding waste among defence officials, including the risk that an arbitrary focus on reaching a certain level of spending could exacerbate this.
The intention is to focus instead on what is necessary – primarily on preparing the UK for a possible war in Europe.

articles.title: Marcos: Singapore visit to help prepare PH industries for the future
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has vowed that his visit to Singapore would help prepare the Philippines for the industries of the future.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 1:51pm
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has vowed that his visit to Singapore would help prepare the Philippines for the industries of the future.
Marcos arrived in Singapore for a five-day working visit on Wednesday, landing at Changi Airport at 11:05 p.m.
"Our objective is not simply to attract investments today. We must ensure that we have the elements that are needed to sustain them in the years ahead," Marcos said in his departure statement.
"I return to Singapore with a clear purpose: to build on one of our most important economic partnerships and prepare our country for the industries of the future," he added.

According to Marcos, this latest Singapore visit will build upon his previous trip to the country last July, where he engaged investors in digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence (AI), healthcare, and more.

The President said this visit has a broader focus now, as he is also set to attend the Forbes Global CEO Conference. At that event, Marcos said he will present the Philippines to investors for opportunities in digital technology, AI, and advanced manufacturing.
Marcos is also set to visit the Singapore Nuclear Research upon the invitation of the Temasek Foundation and Ayala Corporation.

"The Philippines must continue to examine all viable options for our long-term energy security, while developing the knowledge and capabilities needed to make sound decisions for our future," Marcos said.
Marcos' visit to Singapore includes his expected attendance at the Formula 1 race, which Philippine Ambassador to Singapore Medardo Macaraig said will not be paid by Filipino taxpayers.

While the Palace did not confirm whether or not Marcos will watch the sporting event, it maintained that his attendance at the race could present economic investment opportunities for the Philippines. — VDV, GMA News

October 8, 2026
UK's Burnham to meet with Merz in Berlin

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to visit Berlin on Thursday for his first face-to-face meeting with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, during which the two leaders will launch a new UK-Germany joint security partnership.
The partnership aims to counter sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid threats by enhancing information-sharing and establishing coordinated monitoring, deterrence and disruption capabilities.
The initiative comes as Europe is faced by a multitude of hybrid security threats from various adversaries, especially Russia.
Ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat."
"They reach into people's homes and workplaces, and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided," he continued.
"Britain and Germany are joining forces to find, expose and disrupt this activity."
The two leaders are also to discuss support for Ukraine as it faces the ongoing Russian invasion, as well as the conflict in the Middle East and the economic disruption it has caused.
They will also convene a UK-Germany Regional Growth Forum.
The platform aims to bring together British and German chief executives in a bid to promote investment and strengthen industrial partnerships between the two countries.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Trends and Technologies and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Technology-enabled business services and solutions provider Trends & Technologies, Inc. (Trends), together with global connectivity technology leader ReadyLinks, recently hosted a joint event, “Modernizing Networks Without Rebuilding Infrastructure: Smarter Connectivity for High-Demand Environments,” held last September 10 at Solaire in Parañaque City.

The forum introduced Trends and ReadyLinks’s Smart Integrated Resort Solution, an integrated methodology toward modernizing network capabilities for integrated resorts (IRs) and hospitality businesses with a strong emphasis on connectivity, visibility and management, and operational intelligence, and without the need for expensive overhauls.

The Smart Integrated Resort Solution instead focuses on building around existing infrastructure investments, on long-term scalability and ease of deployment with minimal disruption for accommodating growing connectivity requirements.

“The underlying outcome s we’re trying to achieve for IR organizations, in this modernization thrust [with Smart Integrated Resort], is stronger connectivity, more manageable operations, and of course, serviceability for future technologies, without the need overhauls that clients may not be ready for, currently,” said ReadyLinks CEO Larry Synstelien. Synstelien added that IR organizations often move toward having these key improvements:

items: Better visibility across properties
More consistent connectivity across environments, including gaming environments
Simplified management and operations
Support for future technologies and services

blocks.text: And all the above modernization goals should be achieved with reduced disruption during transformation. According to Trends’ converged access infrastructure group head Mark Anthony Castillo, disruption is a key consideration in the Smart Integrated Resort approach.

“Disruption and downtime are crucial consideration s in this approach, as an organization could lose up to $15,000 a minute – that is the average in 2026 for the Global 2000, but the loss is much greater for integrated resorts, especially during peak operational windows. With this threat in mind, our approach should be subtle and most cost-effective,” said Castillo.

“We’re glad we’ve found a strong partner in Trends for the implementation of this approach, which we have developed for the unique needs of the sector, zeroing in on their networks. With our technology, experience in this sector, along with the breadth of expertise of Trends, we’re confident we could achieve these goals for our clients, while also achieving lower costs,” Synstelien said.

The joint forum attests to Trends and ReadyLinks’ commitment to bringing stronger network capabilities to IR operators in the country. In an environment where connectivity is supporting more needs, modernization is crucial for improving hotel and guest services, surveillance and security, retail, dining and event spaces, and gaming and facility operations. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: A youth-led movement is protesting crumbling school buildings and teacher shortages while turning adult focus onto wider educational inequalities

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards.

“School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris, where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today.
“A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters.

Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects. From Paris to the north of England, a similar thread runs through it all: a generation who feel betrayed by the absence of basic economic security and the erosion of public services that older generations took for granted.
I spoke to our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis who has been reporting from the centre of the French protests. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.

Education | Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found.
Spain | María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.
Science | A type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed.
Epstein | British billionaire Sir James Goldsmith warned that Jeffrey Epstein was a “sexual deviant” decades before the FBI closed in on the abuser, a Guardian investigation has found.

blocks.text: In depth: Why have young people taken to the streets?

blocks.caption: ‘School is a right, not a privilege’ … students take to the streets in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: The most significant youth movement to emerge across France in recent decades started on 17 September. Pupils returning to the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, southwest of Paris, after the summer holidays, discovered they couldn’t continue their studies because of the extent of staff absences. The 15- to 18-year-olds blockaded their high school in protest.

After negotiations with the education ministry, those staffing gaps were filled, but the impassioned complaints about crumbling buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days – alongside a wider sense of inequality in the education system – resonated in the suburbs. “This movement grew from the ground up, from teenagers speaking to others outside their lycées. And over a couple of weeks, it has spread to hundreds of schools across France,” Angelique tells me.

There’s a tendency to mythologise youth protest, especially in France – my uncle Joss was in Paris in 1968, and I lapped up his tales of pulling up cobblestones with his bare hands to build barricades. But youth activism is often diminished. When I reported on the schoolchildren who protested against the war in Iraq in 2003, and those who took part in climate strikes more than a decade later, adults repeatedly questioned whether they were swayed by older provocateurs or just wanted an excuse to dodge school and indulge in petty vandalism. (In my experience: no, no and no.)

So it is in France this past month. “This is very much a youth movement,” says Angelique, comparing it to similar protests in 2006 over an unpopular youth employment contract, which were organised by students’ unions. “High schoolers are organising themselves without a centralised system or even spokesperson. That’s historic, and it’s taken the government by surprise.”
Who are the teenagers on the streets?

This week, the sociologist Fabien Truong, who has written widely on youth protest culture, praised the “maturity and coherence” of the protesters. He pointed to a “social media effect” whereby teenagers in wealthier areas were sharing videos of scurrying rats, gaping ceilings and leaking toilets in poorer schools. “It’s beautiful, this solidarity with students from more privileged backgrounds fighting for others and more equality.”

This is precisely what Angelique has witnessed on the streets of Paris in recent days, where some of the most elite state schools have also been barricaded. She spoke to one teacher outside a school in a richer inner-city area, who was proud of her pupils. “She said there was a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers, and how it flies in the face of the idea that they’re part of a social media generation who are selfish and narcissistic.”

“I spent a long time speaking to teenage girls at one of the barricades in the centre of the city,” Angelique says,“who were sitting on top of a pile of bins and shopping trolleys. They told me: ‘We’re told in France that state education is a great leveller, but that’s not the case. We are being taught our lessons, but we’re getting out on to the street because we can’t bear to know that other students in poorer areas are in buildings that are crumbling’.”

***What’s wrong with French schools?As Angelique sets out in this helpful explainer, the pupils’ grievances are backed up by evidence – and the prime minister himself has described them as “legitimate”. Thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, are in need of repair. Class sizes are bigger on average, and school days are longer, than in other comparable countries, while about 10% of teaching hours across the year are not delivered because of absent teachers.

And yet France’s expenditure on high schools is 28% higher than the OECD average. What’s going on? The high spend can be explained in various ways, Angelique tells me. France has a lot more high school buildings to maintain than other countries, and many more vocational courses that cost more to teach.

At the same time, more spending is desperately needed on staff. Teacher shortages are linked to very low pay progression through the profession, while there are severe difficulties in finding teachers to work in deprived areas. There’s also a shortfall in other crucial roles, including school nurses and support staff for pupils with disabilities.
How have adults responded?

Angelique tells me that what has defined how adults are responding to this burgeoning movement is the behaviour of politicians and police. Initially, the French government “had its head in the sand”, she says, distracted by public anger at rising fuel costs and a difficult budget process. “And when it suddenly woke up, the reaction was not a political one, it was a police crackdown.”

Eighteen investigations into possible police brutality are already under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after contact with a stun grenade and a 14-year-old whose jaw was shattered after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher.

Yesterday, the French interior minister suspended the use of stun grenades but rejected accusations of police brutality, saying riot officers only intervened when protesters turned violent. Dozens of teachers have also been injured in clashes, and a small number of schools burned or ransacked, but Angelique tells me that most protests have been peaceful.

The injuries, however, have prompted outrage, with parents and teachers angry at the “disproportionate police response” now joining young people at the barricades. An Elabe poll for BFMTV, published on Wednesday, found that 72% of French people thought the student’s demands were legitimate – although 55% of of those surveyed also thought the protests should come to an end.

The movement has also brought to the fore a debate about the wider state of public services ahead of next year’s presidential election. The radical left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, backed for president by 47% of voters under 35, is loudly supporting the protesters, while far-right candidate Marine Le Pen has blamed the current government for chaos and called for an anti-riot law.

The sheer scale of the marches in cities across France this week was unexpected, Angelique says. “There were hundreds of thousands of parents, grandparents and teachers. There is a lot of support for these young people’s demands and an understanding that the problems they are raising reflect wider worries about public services.”

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Luis Gómez, known as JM, sings with Los Cracks del Puerto at the SCD Hall in Santiago, Chile. Photograph: Tamara Merino/The Guardian

blocks.text: At 65 years old, Luis Gómez was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight. Now at 80, Gomes, or JM as he is popularly known, has become a musical sensation, selling out venues across Chile, as well as in Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France. He is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, who in May released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim.

It’s a long way from his early life in the city of Valparaíso; the youngest of five children, he was three when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he slept on the street between parked cars. JM would eventually form a musical double act with his cousin, Juan Navarro, and the two entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars. The pair would find fame well into their 70s after forming the band in 2017. “I never planned any of this, and I’d be happy still working at the market,” JM says. “But I suppose it’s never too late to give something a try.”

articles.title: PhilHealth underfunding limits improved benefits — solon
articles.summary: According to Montes, the proposed P74.4 billion PhilHealth budget for 2027 falls short from the P75.2 projected collections from sin taxes for tobacco and sweetened beverages alone.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Persistent underfunding has prevented the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. from improving its health benefit packages for its members, a lawmaker said on Thursday, October 8.

House Minority Leader Iris Marie Montes claimed on Thursday, October 8, that the country’s national health insurer has remained underfunded for years even after the passage of the Universal Health Care Act in 2019.

“Sa mga nakaraang taon po, simula po kasi noong naisabatas natin ang Universal Health Care Law, ay mano-notice po natin na hindi po naibibigay nang tama ‘yung pondong dapat sa PhilHealth,” Monte said in an interview with dzMM.
(In the past years, ever since we passed the Universal Health Care Law into law, we have noticed that the appropriate funds for PhilHealth are not properly given.)

The lawmaker also claimed that the mandated earmarks under the law, or the designated funds from sin taxes and shares from the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. (PAGCOR) and the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) for PhilHealth, were not fully and accurately allocated to the agency.
According to Montes, the proposed P74.4 billion PhilHealth budget for 2027 falls short of the P75.2 projected collections from sin taxes for tobacco and sweetened beverages alone.
“Ang nilagay lang po nila tobacco and sweetened beverages; hindi pa nga po kasama ‘yung alcohol and vapor products,” Montes said. “Kulang na nga po ano."
(They only included tobacco and sweetened beverages, not alcohol and vapor products.)
Automatic appropriation
Montes argued that a Supreme Court ruling last year and several measures constitute that under the Universal Healthcare Act, the mandated earmarks must be automatically appropriated to PhilHealth.

The lawmaker was referring to the SC ruling on consolidated petitions on the PhilHealth case in December 2025, ordering the return of a P60-billion excess fund that the Department of Finance (DOF) had ordered to be transferred to the National Treasury.

“With the ruling of the Supreme Court, dapat po malinaw na ito sa DBM (Department of Budget and Management) at sa Kongreso na itong mga earmarks dito ay dapat awtomatikong mapunta sa PhilHealth,” Montes said.
(With the Supreme Court’s ruling, it should be clear to DBM and to Congress that these earmarks must be automatically allotted to PhilHealth.)
Limited benefits
Section 11 of the Universal Health Care Act provides that the PhilHealth must maintain reserve funds with a ceiling of equivalent to two years of projected program expenses.
PhilHealth is required to utilize the excess from these reserve funds to improve the National Health Insurance Program (NHIP) and reduce member contributions.
With the persistent underfunding of PhilHealth, Montes said the public health insurer struggles to provide better health packages and plan for any improvements due to limited financial certainty.

Additionally, the lack of budget predictability, which according to Montes, helps to achieve universal health care, prevents PhilHealth from strategically planning and instead pushes it to reactive spending.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 1:38pm

The Senate on Thursday elected Sen. Mark Villar as a member of the Commission on Appointments and as the chairman of the Senate Committee on Public Works, signaling his move from the minority to the majority.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri moved for the election of Villar to the powerful CA and the public works panel. There were no objections.
Zubiri confirmed that Villar's positions are "as part of the majority."
"Yes. We just elected him to the CA and Public Works committee as part of the majority," Zubiri said.

Villar formally left the minority bloc two weeks after he voted to support a motion to appeal the July 6 decision, which had originally fixed the conviction threshold in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte at 16 votes, representing two-thirds of the entire 24-member Senate.
Following the development, the majority bloc is now composed of 14 members, while the minority has 10 members---four of whom are currently not attending sessions.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, while Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court.
Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, has been on extended medical leave for months now. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Vietnam police arrest 12 over theft of 2,700 cats for slaughter
articles.summary: The group operated mainly between 11 pm and 4 am, using fish bait and traps placed outside homes with pet cats, police say

blocks.text: The group operated mainly between 11 pm and 4 am, using fish bait and traps placed outside homes with pet cats, police say
HANOI, Vietnam – Police in Vietnam have arrested 12 people accused of stealing 2,700 cats and selling them for slaughter in Ho Chi Minh City, the Ministry of Public Security said this week.

items: The suspects, aged between 16 and 39, were arrested on suspicion of stealing the cats with the intention of selling them for food.
The men were found with cat traps, cages and fur-removal equipment, according to a ministry statement.
Police rescued dozens of cats during the raid.
Cat meat dishes are still served in some parts of Vietnam, particularly in rural areas, where they are sometimes marketed as “mini tiger” and believed by some consumers to have medicinal properties
The arrests followed complaints from residents about the nighttime disappearance of their pet cats, the statement said.
Authorities identified Luu Thanh Binh, 39, as the alleged ringleader and distributor. Investigators said he also bought live cats and resold them to customers seeking cat meat.

To supply the operation, Binh allegedly worked with several accomplices who recruited younger people to capture cats in residential neighborhoods. Police said he also supplied traps used in the thefts.
The group operated mainly between 11 pm and 4 am, using fish bait and traps placed outside homes with pet cats. Captured animals were quickly collected and transported for sale, police said.
Police have returned 13 of the cats to their owners and said the remaining animals were being cared for by animal welfare group HavePaws while authorities continued efforts to identify their owners.

articles.title: NSW police commissioner made last-minute bid to hold closed-door hearings into Sydney anti-Herzog protest
articles.summary:
Police watchdog says Mal Lanyon’s timing in raising the issue was ‘regrettable’ and led to delays

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales police commissioner made a last-minute bid to hold hearings into Sydney’s anti-Herzog protest behind closed doors, delaying the inquiry, the police watchdog has revealed.

The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) has said that its inquiry into the February protest at Sydney’s town hall, launched after widespread allegations of police brutality, would go ahead this month with a mix of public and private examinations, saying the timing of issues raised by police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, was “regrettable”.

Lecc launched an investigation after the protest on 9 February, during which numerous protesters – and 10 officers – were injured, including demonstrators in their 70s and 80s. Viral video footage showed police punching multiple protesters, and grabbing Muslim worshippers while they undertook their sunset prayers.
Thirty people were charged in the months after the protest, but four have since had their charges dropped. More than 20 of those charged are due to face a joint hearing next July.

In a decision made public on Thursday, the Lecc chief commissioner, Peter Johnson SC, revealed that legal representatives for Lanyon had indicated for the “first time” on 9 September that he wished to be heard on the issue of public and private examinations. The bid was made less than two weeks before the public hearings between September and November were due to start. Some hearings were also expected to be heard in private.

“The timing of these issues being raised by the Commissioner of Police is more than regrettable given its impact on the orderly progress of the investigation, the preparation for examinations and the efficient and effective use of public resources by both the Commission and the NSWPF and the associated cost and disruption flowing from the delay,” Johnson said.
Johnson said the start date of public hearings, 21 September, was subsequently delayed to “a date to be fixed” to allow a private hearing for submissions on the issue.

Lawyers acting on behalf of Lanyon submitted that Lecc’s opening address and the examination of witnesses should occur in private and not be livestreamed. They argued that the Lecc Act does not have the power to hear “broad ranging open submissions” and said Lecc should not take the “unconventional approach of hearing opening submissions in public part way through an investigation that is already underway”.

But Lecc argued that it does have the power to decide when public examinations are appropriate. The counsel assisting submitted that public examinations were necessary because “there was already significant information concerning the events of 9 February 2026 in the public domain, including footage of use of force by police” and that senior police officers had advanced in public an “official narrative of what took place”.
“Public comments made by senior police increase the need for independent scrutiny,” the commissioner wrote.

The counsel assisting had pointed to specific features of the investigation as reason for why only private examinations were not appropriate. This included the “significant public concern” after the protest, including in parts of the Islamic community in Western Sydney.

On Thursday, the watchdog said its inquiry into the protest would begin with a public address by counsel assisting on 19 October, followed by five weeks of private hearings. Lecc expects senior officers will then appear at public examinations.

It said its Operation Makalu inquiry would analyse the use of OC spray, as well as the “improper use of arrest powers and the police use of force” at the protest. It will consider police planning ahead of the protest and “any opportunities for improvement in the policing of protests”.
after newsletter promotion

In his decision, the commissioner determined that private examinations would be held on “issues of fact” while public examinations would be held to deal with systemic issues, but only after the private examinations have been held.

In September, Palestinian Australian Eyad Shadid launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall. He alleged in his statement of claim that NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution.

In a statement, NSW Greens justice spokesperson, Sue Higginson, described the push to hold hearings in private as “an extraordinary attempt by the police to suppress the public examination of allegations of serious misconduct by uniformed police officers, and to prevent public scrutiny of the political decisions and command structures that led to police violence against protesters”.

At a NSW parliamentary inquiry in May, Johnson said police had become “overly defensive” in response to requests for information in its investigations, describing the relationship between the agencies as “difficult”. He said the Lecc had received a record number of complaints, more than 800, as part of its investigation into the Herzog protest.
In a statement following Johnson’s comments, NSW police said it “complied with the requirements of the LECC Act in a cooperative manner”.
NSW police said in a statement it acknowledged the decision to hold private hearings and awaited the findings.

articles.title: Prosecution: Sara Duterte, husband's undeclared assets not just an error
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio's undeclared assets over the years are not just errors but a willful attempt to conceal information, the House prosecution panel said…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 1:23pm

Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio's undeclared assets over the years are not just errors but a willful attempt to conceal information, the House prosecution panel said Thursday.
“This is willful and deliberate attempt to conceal material information, not just an error or an omission,” House prosecution panel adviser Ace Barbers said in a press conference.
“This is amounting to culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust,” he added.

The prosecution team said over 15 witnesses from banks and insurance firms testified that the Vice President and her husband recorded a range of P35 million to P71 million worth of bank deposits and investment insurance from 2022 to 2025 such as:

items: P59 million in bank deposits, P35.2 million in investment insurance for 2022 (total of P94.2 million)
P71.38 million in bank deposits, P35.9 million in investment insurance for 2023 (total of P107.28 million)
P22.24 million in bank deposits, P59.6 million in investment insurance for 2024 (total of P81.84 million)
P39.09 million in bank deposits, P54 million in investment insurance for 2025 (total of P93.9 million)

blocks.text: Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Adiong said that even if the prosecution will accept the argument of defense counsel Michael Poa that the cash in bank or on hand of the Vice President and her husband were listed under the “others” column in the SALN, the amount listed in “others” will still fall short of the amounts of the bank deposits and investment insurance under the names of the Vice President and her husband.

“They have a P59 million year-end balance in banks in 2022, plus a P35 million insurance. Compare that with P14 million under “others” in their SALN 2022; there’s P80 million undeclared or unexplained. In 2023, their year-end balance in banks is P71 million, plus P35 million investment insurance. Compare that with the “others” entry, which is just at P15 million; there’s still P91 million undeclared in SALN,” Adiong said.

“In 2024, they have P22 million pesos over all the accounts across eight banks, plus P59 million paid in insurance. Compare that with P22 million under “others”; you have P59 million remainder that is unexplained. In 2025, P39 million is the year-end balance in bank accounts, plus P54 million in insurance. They listed P30 million in “others” in SALN, so there’s P63 million still unaccounted for,” he added.
Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr. said that such huge amounts of undeclared assets in multiple years are hard to ignore.

“Hindi lang isang beses na nangyari ito. Paulit-ulit na nangyari across several years. Nakikita natin ngayon ang magnitude ng amounts na pinaguusapan natin. I'm sure the senator judges will take that into consideration,” he said.
(This is not a one-time thing. It was a repeated act across several years. We see the magnitude of the situation.)
Poa earlier said taht Duterte has no cash on hand declared in her official SALN since 2019 because it was "lumped" under the “others” line item.
He added that the Vice President’s cash in bank and even jewelry were also “lumped” all together under that specific line item. —AOL, GMA News

Coalition forces spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said that 82 Houthi military targets had been destroyed in the Yemeni provinces of Saada, Marib, Al Jawf, and Al Hudaydah. Al-Maliki did not provide details about casualties or damage, and his claims could not be independently verified.

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
articles.summary: Pioneering computer scientist led the development of the software for Nasa's Apollo mission and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

blocks.text: The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.

It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.

But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

articles.title: ‘Floating’ money: Did the Dutertes use manager’s checks to hide wealth off bank balances?
articles.summary: 'Repeatedly issuing and cancelling manager’s checks around year-end could therefore raise red flags of reverse window dressing, making bank balances appear smaller without actually reducing wealth,'…

blocks.text: IN AND OUT. Boxes containing evidences lie on the floor before the start of Day 24 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 14, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit

'Repeatedly issuing and cancelling manager’s checks around year-end could therefore raise red flags of reverse window dressing, making bank balances appear smaller without actually reducing wealth,' says global tax policy expert Mon Abrea

items: The prosecution suggested that the use of 'floating' manager's checks linked to Vice President Sara Duterte and former President Rodrigo Duterte was a scheme to make bank balances appear smaller without losing wealth.

Manager's checks, once issued, remove funds from a customer's account until cashed, raising concerns about their use for 'reverse window dressing' if left unused, as it can misrepresent actual financial status.

Experts indicate that it is uncommon for clients to hold large amounts in manager's checks without immediate use, and repeated issuance and cancellation of such checks could signal financial manipulation.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

A mischievously simple theory put forward by the prosecution: Could you move tens of millions of pesos out of a bank account through manager’s checks before year-end, leave the checks unused, and make the account balance look smaller without actually letting go of your wealth?

That is why P96 million in “floating” manager’s checks drew so much attention during the lengthy examination of Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) records involving Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, on Wednesday, October 7.
BPI division head for central Metro Manila branches Marwin Galvez confirmed that two joint time deposits worth around P41 million and P55 million were later converted into manager’s checks.

“A similar time deposit that became a manager’s check in the amount of P55 million was also running during the same years, simultaneously with this P41 million. It’s a total of P96 million,” private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said.

A quick refresher on how manager’s checks (MCs) work. Once a manager’s check is issued, the amount is taken out of the customer’s deposit account and moved to the bank’s settlement account to ensure the check is funded. While that check remains outstanding, the money won’t be reflected in the customer’s bank balance anymore. If it goes unused, the purchaser may later return the unutilized check and get the money back.
Alih called the money “floating,” and when asked by Senator-judge Panfilo Lacson if the prosection was trying to establish a “pattern aimed at proving concealment,” Alih said yes.

Senator-judge Tito Sotto even had a more colorful name for the financial sleight of hand. Citing a banker friend, he said the supposed scheme was called “tinikling” a Philippine folk dance where a dancer goes in and out of moving bamboo poles, although the BPI division head himself said he had never heard the term used in banking.

blocks.caption: ‘Floating’ money: Did the Dutertes use manager’s checks to hide wealth off bank balances?

blocks.text: But is it actually normal for wealthy clients to buy large manager’s checks and then leave them unused?

Rappler asked a senior executive in the wealth management sector about the practice generally. The executive said clients have different reasons for getting manager’s checks, but “usually it’s deposited or paid immediately.”

Rappler has also asked a high-ranking Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas official about safeguards for manager’s checks that remain outstanding for long periods. The official said they were willing to comment, but Rappler had not received a response as of writing.

blocks.caption: LIST: Duterte-Carpio bank accounts, balances detailed in impeachment trial

blocks.text: Global tax policy expert Mon Abrea was even clearer.
“No, it is not common practice. Manager’s checks are generally issued for specific payments, not to temporarily park funds,” he told Rappler.

From an accounting perspective, if an outstanding check has not actually paid anyone and the purchaser still retains ownership or a recoverable claim, Abrea said the amount remains an asset even though the deposit account has already been debited.

“Repeatedly issuing and cancelling manager’s checks around year-end could therefore raise red flags of reverse window dressing, making bank balances appear smaller without actually reducing wealth,” he said.
If a manager’s check paid a loan, it should reflect in the reduced amount of liability. If it bought an investment, the asset changes form. So what happens if a manager’s check remains unencashed?
“Substance over form – it is still cash to be added back to bank balance so sa (in the) total cash, it should still be there,” he told Rappler.
All this goes back to the discussion of the Vice President’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he checked Sara Duterte’s 2010 and 2011 SALNs – back when she was still vice mayor and then mayor of Davao City – and could not find the P96 million in joint time deposits reflected there.

blocks.caption: ‘Floating’ money: Did the Dutertes use manager’s checks to hide wealth off bank balances?

blocks.text: The defense, however, stressed that the documents presented in court carried Rodrigo Duterte’s signature, not Sara’s. Her lawyer Michael Poa said the Vice President did not recall the account, while BPI testimony showed her father could transact on the joint account without her participation. (READ: Is Sara Duterte unaware of BPI accounts with father Rodrigo?)

This was actually not the first time manager’s checks came up in the BPI money trail. Several MCs also appeared in records tied to a separate controversy involving BPI’s request for the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) to delete 13 transaction reports after what the bank called a “system bug” inflated transaction records involving Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio. The inaccurate amounts triggered covered transaction reports. – Rappler.com
