articles.title: Isaias expected to become hurricane before hitting U.S. Gulf Coast, forecasters say
articles.summary: Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters predicted it will quickly strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before striking the…

image.caption: A satellite image from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows Tropical Storm Isaias off the eastern coast of Mexico on Wednesday. (U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters predicted it will quickly strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before striking the U.S. Gulf Coast later in the week.
Landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening

Communities in the potential path of Isaias moved quickly to prepare, with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening. Some Gulf oil wells paused production and an Alabama beach city cancelled a weekend festival known to draw thousands of tourists. Florida's governor declared a state of emergency for more than one-third of the state's counties.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday's college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, which U.S. President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
Isaias could become a major Category 3 hurricane, with winds of 178 km/h or stronger, before it strikes land, said Michael Brennan, director of the U.S. National Hurricane Center.
"We're expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast beginning Friday and continuing into the weekend," Brennan said in a video briefing Wednesday.
A late arrival

The storm was on track to tie or break a 121-year-old record as the latest arriving initial hurricane of the Atlantic season. According to the U.S. National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year's first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.

The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year due to a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity in the Pacific has been above average, where Tropical Storm Simon also formed Wednesday off Mexico.

The Miami-based hurricane centre on Wednesday issued a hurricane watch for the northern Gulf Coast from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on the Florida Panhandle. The watch means hurricane conditions are possible within 48 hours.

items: Polo makes 2nd landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo

blocks.text: Brennan says dangerous storm surge could affect an even wider area, from southeast Louisiana to Florida's Big Bend. Heavy rains of seven to 15 centimetres could trigger flash flooding near the coast, with accumulations of three to eight centimetres as far inland as Tennessee and the western Carolinas.

Isaias was centred about 365 kilometres northwest of Progreso, Mexico, and about 805 kilometres south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the hurricane center. It had maximum sustained winds of 100 km/h and was moving east-northeast at 13 km/h.

Forecasters predict Isaias will become a hurricane by Thursday as it turns north toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. Though its path and timing could shift, the storm is expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday.

Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that's no stranger to major hurricanes. One of the 20th century's worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Miss., in 1969.
Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighbourhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael levelled homes and buildings near Panama City, Fla., in 2018.
Gulf oil production, tourism already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 per cent of crude pumped annually in the U.S.

As of Wednesday, producers had temporarily halted about 25 per cent of the oil produced in the region, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.

With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect oil markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
"I would characterize the oil market risk as moderate, but rising," Burkhard said in an email.
In Gulf Shores, Ala., the storm threat caused organizers to cancel the National Shrimp Festival scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state's emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment.

In Pensacola, on the Panhandle, electric utilities were readying crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding.

articles.title: Rubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approach
articles.summary:
In the shadow of the Parthenon, the secretary of state gave a selective reading of history as he urged Europe to ‘awaken from its slumber’

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a…

blocks.text: The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a classically inspired apologia for Donald Trump’s “America first” foreign policy on Wednesday, giving a sweeping speech to the backdrop of the Parthenon in Athens that appeared tailor-made for campaign ads if he runs for president in 2028.

In the speech, the top US diplomat drew historical parallels from the founders, philosophers and conquerers of antiquity to the modern American spirit – as well as his family’s own journey to the United States – as he called on Europe to “awaken from its long slumber” and reject a “future of atrophy and servitude and decline”.

The highly produced speech contained a forceful rejection of the kind of globalist politics that Trump has blamed for America’s and Europe’s ills, including growing illegal immigration and the outsourcing of manufacturing. In it, Rubio warned that the western world was at an “inflection point” and defended America’s “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.

“The word nationalism became a dirty word, so we tore down our monuments,” Rubio said. “We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the country they would inherit.”
Now, he said, the western world had found itself at a crossroads, where it either must “maintain its place at the head of the world or [resign] itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline”.

“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice,” Rubio continued. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.”

The speech comes as relations between the US and Europe are facing numerous strains, including the US war in Iran, Washington’s scattershot support for Ukraine’s defense against Russia, disputes inside Nato including Trump’s recent demands for sovereignty over Greenland, and a growing ideological divide being driven by powerful officials including the US vice-president, JD Vance.

The shift in the Trump administration’s use of national power has unsettled many European allies, who have continued to seek compromises in order to keep the Trump administration onside on major issues including support for Ukraine and economic cooperation through the European Union.

Vance, a likely contender in the 2028 elections, put European allies on notice last year in a speech at the Munich security conference, when he accused leaders of being “terrified of their own people” and warned about the “threat from within” that Europe would reject values it shared with the US.
Rubio has developed a less aggressive – but nonetheless pointed – message of calling for European powers led by the US to fight against “civilisational erasure”.

Rubio addressed the tensions as he invoked Abraham Lincoln’s first inaugural address in 1861 on the eve of the civil war, saying: “Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them.”

“Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age,” he said, extolling the recent agreement between the US, Denmark, and Greenland that he claimed will “reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of Nato.”

But the speech on Wednesday indicates that the shift in US geopolitical power may remain through a following presidency, as two of the most prominent Republican officials in the current administration have delivered forceful declarations to Europe that there will not be a return to the politics of the past.

On Wednesday, speaking to a crowd of 250 invited Greek and European officials, as well as journalists, Rubio sought to rally European allies, saying they should follow the example of the current government of Greece, to embrace a partnership with the US on everything from “everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally”.

“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” Rubio said, pointing to positive tendencies including increases in European defense spending, expanded manufacturing and production, and a “flurry” of new partnerships and programs.

To bolster his case, Rubio delivered a selective reading of history from antiquity to the present, saying that the values of the Ancient Greeks imbued those of later scientists and explorers, including some controversial choices including Christopher Columbus and the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés, whose legacies are associated with the subjugation of Latin America.
But Rubio said they, as well as many others, carried a frontier spirit that was born in antiquity.

“The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world,” he said.

The Acropolis speech was heavily produced, with four cameras including one mounted on a crane, and was unusual for a secretary of state delivering a speech during a three-country swing through Iceland, Portugal and finally Greece.
In an unusual aside for the US’s top diplomat, Rubio also linked his own journey back to Europe, and then back to the Greeks of antiquity as well.

“Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the secretary of state of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish,” he said.

articles.title: Why more than 250,000 people have joined student-led protests in France
articles.summary: France has been thrown into crisis as student-led protests erupted across the nation, calling for better conditions for learning and for the government to address a decade-long staffing shortage.…

image.caption: France has been thrown into crisis as student-led protests erupted across the nation, calling for better conditions for learning and for the government to address a decade-long staffing shortage. Students, pictured here in Bordeaux on Oct. 6, hold placards reading 'Surviving or studying' on the left

blocks.text: France has been thrown into crisis as student-led protests erupted across the nation, calling for better conditions for learning and for the government to address a decade-long staffing shortage.

Protests began at a Paris-region high school in mid-September, soon growing into a nationwide movement. More than 250,000 people took to the streets on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, the Interior Ministry said, in the demonstration's biggest day yet. (Organizers put the number higher, at 450,000.)

The rallies have led to widespread school disruptions, arrests and violence, with police deploying tear gas and other riot-control weapons against crowds of mainly teenagers — angering their parents and teachers and prompting them to participate.

It represents the latest test for outgoing President Emmanuel Macron. His prime minister Sébastien Lecornu addressed the nation on Wednesday night, pledging to introduce new measures by the end of the month. A platform for students to voice grievances, launched on Tuesday, has already received some 40,000 submissions.
Here's a look at what we know so far about the protests — and how they became so widespread.
Protesters hold a banner reading 'Rostand angry, Rostand supportive' during the protest in Caen, France, on Oct. 6. (Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images)
Why are they protesting?

Many high school students say the state of their learning environment is poor, from decaying infrastructure to a lack of personnel. More than half of all schools are short-staffed this year, according to a survey conducted by a secondary school teachers’ union.

The shortage has affected public education in France for close to a decade. The chronic failure to replace absent teachers or hire substitutes means students can miss hundreds of hours of instruction.

items: India’s Cockroach Party shows frustrated Gen-Zers are hard to crush
Anti-government protesters clash with riot police in Mexico City during Gen Z-led rally

blocks.text: They are fed up with overcrowded classrooms, as well, which have increased to an average of 25 to 30 students a class.

Students also describe dilapidated buildings, pest infestations — including cockroaches and rats — and uninsulated classrooms severely affected by temperature shifts, particularly during recent heat waves.
“In the summer, it's 35 degrees,” said Rudy Cuvilliez, who studies in the Paris suburb of Pantin. “And we're, like, 30 to 35 students in every class, so it's unbearable!”
Rudy Cuvilliez, who studies in the Paris suburb of Pantin, holds up canisters from tear gas he says police fired earlier in the day on Oct. 6. (Kyle G. Brown/CBC)

Students and their supporters have taken to the streets for weeks because they feel the government is doing too little, too late. The Education Ministry will receive an additional €1.2 billion in funding next year, but it will not be enough, according to opposition parties, who say the amount barely keeps up with inflation.
Why is the state of schools so poor?
The French state spends more on education than on any other ministry, but it has not kept up with a sharp increase in the youth population, expected to peak in 2028.

The movement originated in the suburbs of the greater Paris region — areas historically underserved and facing significant growth. There are considerable regional disparities, with Île-de-France spending less than any other region in the country.
Schools in higher-income areas benefit from parents’ contributions, while those in underprivileged areas often lack resources.
Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting
Meanwhile, administrative and contracting procedures can be complex, meaning that even repairs that have been financed can take a long time to carry out.
As for personnel, teachers are not valued as they once were — entry-level salaries were more than double minimum wage in 1980; now, they are only just above the minimum.

“The government has not really made an effort to make the profession attractive," said Agnès Van Zanten, a senior research professor emeritus at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research, "such as by raising salaries, for instance.”

items: Gen Z toppled Bangladesh's autocratic regime. Will it decide the next government?

blocks.text: What do the students want?

Many want to see large-scale recruitment of teachers, school nurses and teaching assistants. Students, particularly in the banlieues, or economically deprived suburbs, call for urgent repairs and renovations to school buildings.
Recent educational reforms have resulted in longer school days, often extending from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., which many find onerous.

But students should be careful what they wish for: The French school day is so long in part to compensate for lengthy school vacations — some 16 weeks compared to the European average of 14. Shortening school days may mean fewer holidays.
A protester in Paris holds a sign that says, 'Is the revolution reserved for history classes?' in French on Oct. 6. (Kyle G. Brown/CBC)

What keeps other students awake at night is “Parcoursup,” a national web platform where high schoolers can secure a place in a higher education institution. Students can list up to 10 schools of preference, with their marks and test results included in their applications.
How they are assessed, however, is a bit of a mystery, with critics calling for the repeal or overhaul of the process.
It was among the topics raised by students meeting with the national education minister last week, but they reached no agreement, and school blockades resumed.
Wracked by weeks of student protests and an increasingly broad base of support, the French government is now trying to rush through a number of reforms.
What disruptions have the protests caused?

Since the movement began last month, hundreds of schools have been blockaded. And while the majority of protests have been peaceful, some have been marred by vandalism and violence. Police have made more than 5,000 arrests so far.
More than 200 people have been injured since the student mobilization began, “whether in accidents … or due to injuries caused by troublemakers,” said Education Minister Édouard Geffray.
Up to 500 schools in France to remain closed amid student protests

Police have also severely injured some people, including a youth who was blinded in one eye after being hit by a flash-ball. France has suspended the use of stun grenades after 15-year-old boy's hand was mutilated in northern France.

Amnesty International condemned “the disproportionate use of force against secondary school protests," calling for police to de-escalate. At least 18 internal police investigations are underway into alleged police violence.
Why has the response been so aggressive?

The Interior Ministry is applying a policy of “absolute firmness” to break up blockades and prevent the destruction of public property. Twenty-four schools had been burned or ransacked on Sunday, according to the education minister.

French police forces have often been criticized by human rights groups and the UN for their use of excessive force, and the response to the student protests has sparked intense controversy, not least among parents.
Teenager loses hand in violent France school protests

items: Police in France use tear gas, water cannons against student protesters
Macron government struggles to quell protests as riot police clash with high schoolers

blocks.text: Critics blame the prime minister and interior minister for inciting the police by insisting the movement was a problem of social order rather than trying to address students’ demands.
Why is the government worried about these protests?

Even though most of the protesters are under 18 — the minimum voting age in France — the government still sees the continued uprising as a threat to public order, particularly now that parents, teachers and activists of all kinds have joined in solidarity.

Indeed, the government is concerned about a potential “coalition of anger,” in which frustration with a decade under Macron reaches a boiling point. Historically in France, youth movements have often served as a catalyst for wider social movements and upheaval.

articles.title: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after botched execution
articles.summary: Pike's lawyers have said she was very aware of Tennessee's failed execution effort. A judge has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence from the botched execution.

image.caption: Pike's lawyers continue to demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute her sentence to life in prison and never reattempt her executionImage: George Walker IV/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A US judge told the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed attempt to execute Christa Pike, whom lawyers say is "angry and confused" after waking up in hospital nearly a week after the ordeal.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for torturing and killing classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, survived despite being given two lethal doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug.
What do we know about Christa Pike's current state?
One of her attorneys spoke about the 50-year-old's state after the failed execution.
"She is angry and confused about everything right now," Randy Spivey said during a news conference, adding Pike is "very aware" of what was done to her.

"She cannot move either of her arms, both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms," Spivey said, adding that "there's a long road ahead" for her recovery.
Pike is the only person known to have survived after receiving lethal injection drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike, said that "medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request."

Her lawyers continue to demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike's sentence to life in prison and never reattempt her execution. The Republican governor had denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution.

blocks.caption: Demonstrations were held against Christa Pike's executionImage: George Walker IV/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pike's recovery period unclear
Experts say it is possible that the failed execution was due to a problem with the IV line that caused the injection to pool in her tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.
"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown," her attorneys wrote in their court filing.

Pike's arms were burned and blistered due to the injection, according to her legal team, who are demanding that the prison authority holds all information from the attempted execution, including needles and execution logs.
It is not yet clear how Pike's recovery might unfold and whether she will be subjected to another execution attempt.

articles.title: ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins
articles.summary:
People tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensive


Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke

blocks.text: Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions.

Ishtaiwi lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in central Gaza with his two daughters. Their former home is far to the north, in the now ruined town of Beit Lahiya, uninhabitable and impossible to reach.

blocks.caption: Ahmed Ishtaiwi, 43, from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in southern Gaza.  Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian
Ahmed Ishtaiwi’s chairs are among his most valuable possessions. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: “When I sit on those chairs, I remember sitting in the garden at home, having breakfast and drinking tea. They remind me of my life there,” he said last week.

Wednesday is the anniversary of the raid on 7 October 2023 by Hamas militants into southern Israel that killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and triggered a relentless Israeli military offensive that killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounded many more and reduced swathes of Gaza to rubble.

When Layan al-Jbour, a 15-year-old from the southern city of Khan Younis, tries to bring some order to the crowded makeshift shelter she shares with her parents, brothers and sisters in al-Mawasi, a strip of coastline at the southernmost end of Gaza, she recalls life before the war.

“When I tidy the tent, I remember our home and how I used to tidy it. I remember my room and how I used to make my bed. When I put a sheet over a table and arrange the bedding, the place looks like our old home,” al-Jbour said.

blocks.caption: Layan al-Jbour, 15, from Khan Younis holds up a cardiology report from a hospital. The only item she took with her was her schoolbag. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We hardly took anything with us from our home. We left everything behind, and the only thing I took was my schoolbag. It is the most precious thing I own now. It reminds me so much of my school days. I loved going to school and meeting my friends there.”

Across Gaza, Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges that nothing in their former lives prepared them for: shortages of water and of nourishing food, minimal healthcare, disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the continuing threat of death or injury.

Despite a ceasefire a year ago, Israel’s airstrikes continue. Palestinians who have approached the “yellow line” that divides Gaza into zones controlled by the Israeli military and by Hamas have been shot dead. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people.
In recent days, Israeli attacks have intensified, killing at least two Palestinians in Gaza on Tuesday, according to health officials. The Israeli military said the strikes targeted militants.
On Wednesday, Gaza medics said at ​least two Palestinians were killed and others wounded in airstrikes in Beit Lahiya and Khan Younis.

blocks.caption: Palestinians gather at the site of an Israeli airstrike that killed a Palestinian in a camp in Khan Younis on Wednesday. Photograph: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “It is what we feared … a ceasefire that just isn’t a ceasefire,” said one international aid worker now based in Amman, Jordan, who worked in Gaza throughout much of the conflict. “Daily life is horrible. People aren’t hungry any more but they are still malnourished. Our local staff are telling us that this is just the next stage of the conflict.”

Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told the UN security council last month that despite the increase in supplies entering Gaza, the health situation remained critical, with “infectious diseases … widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions”.

Inadequate funding for relief efforts exacerbated the “shortages of medical supplies, fuel and the overall humanitarian response”, Alakbarov said, while “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items imposed by Israel” were slowing preparations for cold weather.
Israeli authorities deny shortages and say adequate supplies are reaching Gaza, with more than 600 trucks entering the territory each day.

blocks.caption: Saleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, lives in a camp in Deir al-Balah in southern Gaza. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Saleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, used to have a farm and olive trees before the war. “Around this time of year, I used to press about 60 containers of olive oil. But I lost all of that too. If I go to my home I may die, and if I go to my farm, I may die too. This is not a life. We are exhausted and we have lost hope.”

Kilani said life before the conflict seemed very distant. “We never used to think twice about seeing orange and peach trees, green fields, grapes and figs. These things were simply part of our lives. Now when we see them, we are surprised,” he said.

Hamas, which swiftly reimposed its authority over the 2.3 million Palestinians who live in the third of Gaza not under the control of the Israeli military, has rebuilt a rudimentary administration which provides patchy education, some healthcare services and limited policing based on deterrence through often arbitrary punishment.

Donald Trump’s plan to definitively end the war in Gaza has stalled, with little progress towards disarming Hamas, securing the withdrawal of Israeli troops and beginning the vast job of reconstruction.
“My biggest fear is that this situation will continue. We are living through a period that can be described as neither war nor peace,” said Kilani.
The only time Esraa Abu Taiba recalls her prewar existence is when she gets to practise her former profession: beautician.

blocks.caption: Esraa Abu Taiba, 26, from Bani Suheila to the east of Khan Younis, used to work as a beautician in her former life. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: The 26-year-old lived in Bani Suheila, a town to the east of Khan Younis and now within the zone controlled by Israel. Of her five brothers, two were killed in the conflict, two were wounded, and one is among the more than 1,500 Palestinians from Gaza in detention in Israel.

“Before the war my life was quiet and good,” she said. “I could go wherever I wanted without fear or restrictions. We lived in our own home. We had a washing machine, a tap and a garden. The house belonged to us and we lived there comfortably.

“Now we live in a tent. Our lives depend on carrying water and getting food from the community kitchen. A water truck comes to the end of the street and … I go to collect it because my mother cannot carry it.”
Like most Palestinians in Gaza, her family was displaced multiple times during the conflict, and they have lost everything from their former home – except a house key, which her mother keeps close.
“The only thing I still do from my old life is some beauty work. I cut girls’ hair in the tents around us and do their makeup for weddings,” said Abu Taiba.

“It takes me back to a beautiful and happy period of our lives, when we used to celebrate weddings and other happy occasions before the war. It takes me away from the misery we are living through, even if only for a little while.”

articles.title: Texas set to carry out first US execution since botched lethal injection of Christa Pike
articles.summary:
Jamaal Howard’s lawyers urge halt, citing risk of another failed execution after Pike’s ordeal in Tennessee

Texas on Wednesday is scheduled to carry out the first execution in the US after…

blocks.text: Texas on Wednesday is scheduled to carry out the first execution in the US after the the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.
Lawyers for Jamaal Howard, a Texas man on death row for capital murder, are seeking to halt the execution, arguing there are similar risks as in the case of Pike.
Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in 2001 for robbing a convenience store in Silsbee, a town north of Beaumont, and fatally shooting 42-year-old clerk Vickie Swartout.
His legal team has also argued that, at the time of the crime, Howard was intellectually disabled and thus ineligible for the death penalty, as the supreme court ruled in 2002.

Pike survived two doses of barbiturate pentobarbital, the same sedative Texas officials plan to administer to Howard. Pike had complained her arms felt like they were going to explode as she was given the drug.
She regained consciousness on Tuesday. Her lawyers say she has pneumonia and is unable to move her arms.

blocks.caption: Jamaal Howard in this Texas department of criminal justice handout. Photograph: Texas department of criminal justice/AP

blocks.text: Pike’s was the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, and governor Bill Lee has barred any further lethal injections for the rest of the year. He has also ordered a probe into why Pike’s execution failed. Pike’s lawyers had previously argued her blood disorder would make a lethal injection painful. Speculation has also swirled over the quality of the pentobarbital.

“There is a similar risk,” Howard’s attorneys wrote in a Wednesday motion filed with Texas’s court of criminal appeals, “that Texas’s execution drugs are likewise degraded, as they are far past the original beyond-use dates that the pharmacopeia allows for drugs of this kind.”
Howard’s Wednesday appeal comes a week after the fifth circuit court of appeals declined a request to stop Howard’s execution.
The motion said Howard’s attorneys had filed requests for information about the lethal dose of pentobarbital the Texas department of criminal justice planned to use.
The Texas attorney general opinion is not expected to be returned until after Wednesday, meaning Howard cannot litigate whatever decision the state might make on releasing that information, they say.
Texas officials did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday morning.

articles.title: María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87
articles.summary: Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis
articles.byline: Ashifa Kassam and Sam Jones in Madrid

blocks.text: María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.
News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain, was evicted from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than seven decades.
The pensioner, whose apartment had been purchased by an investment firm who sought to hike her rent by 230%, swiftly became a symbol of the many left behind by Spain’s surging housing market.

Scenes of the eviction, which saw police use rounds of teargas as they carried out the order, made headlines across Spain. The shocking images – showing Abascal being forcibly removed from her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police – swiftly crystallised into anger.

About 10,000 people took to the streets of Madrid hours later, wielding signs such as “Shame” and “We’re all Maricarmen”. From Spain’s north to the south, people poured into plazas to protest the suffering wrought by rents that had soared 80% in the span of a decade while house prices had climbed 63%.

blocks.caption: A flyer with an image of María del Carmen Abascal is seen at a vigil in Madrid on 7 October.  Photograph: Thomas Coex/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: From the hospital where she was being treated for severe exhaustion, Abascal cheered on the fledgling movement. “I would like to be there with you all,” she said in a video shot from her hospital bed. “But I’m not that lucky. So from here, I ask you all for courage and to fight and defend what is yours.”

As encampments began springing up across the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return. The deal did little to quell the anger that had boiled over in the wake of the eviction.

This week the wave of outrage led the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap general election after rightwing and far-right parties voted down two emergency decrees his government had proposed to address the housing crisis.

The Madrid tenants’ union said the solution had come too late for the octogenarian. “This was a completely preventable situation following an agonising ordeal,” it said in a statement announcing that Abascal had died in hospital, reportedly hours before she was due to sign a new lease with the investment firm that had evicted her.

“The events triggered by the injustice of her eviction undoubtedly mark a turning point in the history of this country: massive demonstrations, encampments in the squares, an early election, and the call for a general strike,” it added. “The housing debate is at the center of it all, but the cost of getting to this point has been too high.”
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”

Spain’s health minister, Mónica García, said Abascal’s plight had “served to awaken awareness across all of Spain, lighting a fuse that cannot be put out”, and adding that her “dignity and courage” had shown the way.

blocks.caption: María del Carmen Abascal in Madrid on 2 June. Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Podemos MEP and former equalities minister Irene Montero was more blunt. “This isn’t a death; it’s a murder,” she wrote on social media. “Such bloody anger. Thank you for fighting, Maricarmen.”
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP) – which voted against last week’s emergency housing measures – also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”

Her death came a day after Sánchez’s cabinet approved two new housing decrees intended to “maintain the spirit” of the two previous decrees that were voted down in parliament last week by the PP, the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party.

The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; regulating room rentals; imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases; and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.

With the lower and upper houses of parliament dissolved following the calling of the snap election, the decrees will be voted on by the permanent council of congress, a special council that operates when parliament is not in session.

The body’s 69 members are distributed proportionally among the various parliamentary groups to reflect the composition of the lower chamber, meaning Sánchez will probably have enough support to get at least one of the decrees passed.

In the heart of Madrid, where campaigners have set up a giant protest camp, news of Abascal’s death was met with a moment of silence. Soon after, hundreds marched from the camp to the country’s parliament chanting: “Maricarmen lives on, the fight continues.”

articles.title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
articles.summary: Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years in September.

blocks.text: An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.

Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours,'" it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Protesters gathered at one of Madrid's main squares, Puerta del Sol, following the announcement of Abascal's death. The site has become a protest encampment for protesters over the last two weeks.
Photos show demonstrators lighting candles and holding posters of Maricarmen at the housing protest camp on Wednesday evening.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.

articles.title: Canada yanks sponsorship of disinformation conference discussing U.S. as a threat
articles.summary: The federal government has withdrawn sponsorship of a European disinformation conference that includes panels discussing the U.S. government as a foreign interference risk.

image.caption: Canadian and European diplomatic services pulled their support for a disinformation conference in Lithuania's capital on Wednesday. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The federal government has withdrawn sponsorship of a European disinformation conference that includes panels discussing the U.S. government as a foreign interference risk.
Global Affairs says it took issue with the framing of some of panels

Samantha Lafleur, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada (GAC), said the government took issue with the framing of some panels at the event organized by EU DisinfoLab, a non-profit based in Brussels.

The conference features panels about the U.S. as a source of "foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI)," a phenomenon where foreign governments or actors on their behalf manipulate information to confuse, divide or mislead the public and erode confidence in institutions.

GAC — Ottawa's diplomatic arm — Lithuania's Foreign Ministry and the European External Action Service were initially listed as supporters of the annual conference largely attended by researchers and civil society organizations.
The government of Canada logo was covered up on signs spotted around the anti-disinformation conference. (Submitted)

As the gathering got underway in Vilnius, Lithuania, on Wednesday, their names were covered up on signs spotted around the conference, according to photos shared with CBC News. As of writing, the French government remains a sponsor.
In a statement to CBC News, GAC did not deny that it had concerns with describing the U.S. as a foreign interference threat.
"Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference," wrote Lafleur.
She did not respond to questions about particular changes GAC took issue with or whether the U.S. raised concerns.

According to the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, the description of Wednesday's panel discussing how to push back on the U.S. as a foreign interference threat appears to have been unchanged since Sept. 9.
GAC no longer chairing Arctic panel
A GAC official also pulled out of chairing a session on disinformation in the Arctic scheduled for Thursday, said presenter Ben Shultz with the American Sunlight Project.
The panel proposes to talk about Greenland and "growing evidence that the United States has, in specific Arctic contexts, operated as a FIMI actor."
Shultz shared the initial plan for the panel from months ago, which includes talking about the U.S. as a foreign interference actor.
He called three governments withdrawing a "shock" and questioned whether they were pressured.

"Thankfully every speaker has still shown up, which is awesome, and I think a testament to the resolve of the research community. But it's definitely put a bit of a damper on the atmosphere," he said in an interview.

items: Past Alberta separatist meetings in U.S. don't fall under foreign influence registry: watchdog
Liberal government targets deepfakes, foreign interference in major election law reforms

blocks.text: The European External Action Service, the EU's diplomatic service, said in a statement it asked to have its logo removed from the material associated with the conference "in view of the content of the programme."

Asked if it was related to the U.S. foreign interference panel, an EU spokesperson repeated that the EEAS logo was removed because "organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU."
Neither Lithuania's Foreign Ministry nor the conference organizers responded to a request for comment.
Canada's withdrawal comes the same week the Globe and Mail reported that some people involved in campaigning for Alberta independence had met on both sides of the border with U.S. entities.
CBC News previously reported that some of those meetings took place in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.
GAC's move also comes as the country is embroiled in an often bitter and personal trade dispute with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.

Lafleur said Canada "remains firmly committed to addressing the challenge of disinformation and misinformation" and that Global Affairs Canada officials "look forward to engaging with partners and stakeholders on efforts to counter disinformation."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catharine Tunney is a reporter with CBC's Parliament Hill bureau, where she covers national security and the RCMP. She worked previously for CBC in Nova Scotia. You can reach her at catharine.tunney@cbc.ca

articles.title: 'Crypto King' investor who lost $890K recounts visit to Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion
articles.summary: Stewart Wilson testified it felt like "TV stuff" as he sat in self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion five years ago and the young man told him he was operating a $30-$50…

image.caption: 27-year-old Aiden Pleterski walking into the Superior Court of Justice building on Monday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto

Stewart Wilson testified it felt like "TV stuff" as he sat in self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion five years ago and the young man told him he was operating a $30-$50 million investment fund.
Witness testified Pleterski went from renting luxury cars from him to owning within 2 years

Stewart Wilson testified it felt like "TV stuff" as he sat in self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion five years ago as he told him he was operating a $30-$50 million investment fund.
"It was about 8,000 square feet on the waterfront in Burlington. At that point you could peg it at eight million dollars," Wilson told the court.
"He told me he bought it. I told him he was crazy."
Wilson, who ended up investing $890,000 with Pleterski, was called as a witness for the Crown in the now 27-year-old’s fraud and money laundering trial Wednesday in Superior Court in Toronto.
Pleterski has pleaded not guilty to both charges.

The Crown is alleging Pleterski guaranteed investors' money given to him for trading between July 2020 and July 2022, but never actually invested the funds. Instead, the Crown argues Pleterski spent the money on himself: Exotic cars, flights on private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions.
'He had been raking in a lot of money'

About a year and half before Wilson’s November 2021 mansion visit, he testified that Pleterski showed up at his business, GTA Exotics, which rents out luxury cars. He said Pleterski "started out small," renting an Audi R8. From there, Pleterski went on to rent out higher-end sports cars like Lamborginis and a McLaren.
Eventually, Wilson said Pleterski stopped renting and he said he believed Pleterski had bought his own Audi.
"I saw through social media he was doing well, living in this big house ... he bought some very extravagant cars, I was happy for him," Wilson testified.
"He didn’t try to entice me at all into joining, which I thought was pretty cool, he was doing it on his own."

After seeing that, and hearing Pleterski’s close friends and family were investing and hearing they were getting returns, Wilson says he reached out to Pleterski to catch up and was invited to Pleterski’s Burlington, Ont. mansion.

Wilson said Pleterski told him he was paying a $49,000 monthly mortgage and that he saw a many of "the newest Lamborghinis," worth roughly $600,000 each, at the property, as well as a McLaren he estimated would be worth $2 million in Pleterski’s garage.
He also said Pleterski told him the investment fund he was trading with was now between $30-$50 million.

Stewart Wilson testified that Pleterski showed up at his business, GTA Exotics, and rented out an Audi R8. Pleterski went on to rent higher-end sports cars like Lamborginis and a McLaren. (Aiden Pleterski/YouTube)
"I’m literally sitting in his living room doing the math. How much he’s paying for his mortgage, how much he paid for these cars," Wilson said. "He had been raking in a lot of money."

After the meeting, Wilson decided to start investing with Pleterski and signed an initial investment contract for $300,000. A copy of it was shown in court and it included a guarantee that the principal investment would be returned over time if the money was lost.
"Everything just made sense. It was smooth. It made me feel very comfortable. So that’s why we invested," said Wilson.
"I considered him a friend. And his closest friends were investing with him, that I knew."

Wilson went on to invest another $590,000 over four more contracts between November 2021 and February 2022. Wilson said Pleterski told him he was investing in gold and foreign exchange, not cryptocurrency. Wilson said he didn’t trust cryptocurrency and wouldn’t invest in it.

The court was shown text messages between the pair where Pleterski would update Wilson on the percentage of returns that week and also spreadsheets on each of the investments. One of those spreadsheets showed a $100,000 investment in mid-December 2021 more than doubled to about $241,300 by the end of March.
Exotic cars and private jets: Inside day one of the 'Crypto King' trial
'I need a lawyer': Pleterski
In March, Wilson tried to get some of his money out. The jury saw text messages from Pleterski stringing him along for weeks — saying the money was coming, but it never did.
"Did you ever receive that money back?" Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson asked Wilson.
"Nothing," Wilson responded.

Pleterski, who is representing himself at trial, told the court he did not have any questions for Wilson. He also decided not to cross-examine another investor, Olesya Chornenka, earlier Wednesday morning.
Pleterski told the judge, "I don’t have any questions, I need a lawyer."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: How much sugar is in these 'sugar-free' Starbucks protein drinks? As much as a candy bar, claims lawsuit
articles.summary: Starbucks has been sued by U.S. consumers who said the coffee chain falsely advertised eight protein beverages as "sugar-free" because they contain lactose, a naturally occurring sugar in milk.

image.caption: A Starbucks store in Boston in this February photo. A lawsuit filed Friday in a Seattle federal court accuses Starbucks of trying to capitalize on 'the protein craze' and nutritional preferences of customers. (Charles Krupa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
Starbucks has been sued by U.S. consumers who said the coffee chain falsely advertised eight protein beverages as "sugar-free" because they contain lactose, a naturally occurring sugar in milk.
U.S. lawsuit says coffee chain falsely advertised eight protein beverages as 'sugar-free'
It's fair to say you probably have some idea what you're in for, sugar-wise, when you order a pumpkin spice latte or caramel macchiato from Starbucks.
But what should you expect if you're ordering a drink that's labelled "sugar-free?"

That's the question behind a proposed U.S. class-action lawsuit that claims the coffee chain falsely advertised eight protein beverages as "sugar-free," when they actually contain between 13 and 21 grams of sugar per venti-size serving due to the naturally occurring sugar in milk.
The lawsuit, filed Friday in a Seattle federal court and viewed by CBC News, accuses Starbucks of trying to capitalize on "the protein craze" and nutritional preferences of customers.

"By naming its beverages 'Sugar-Free,' Starbucks makes a specific, quantitative and verifiable claim about the nature of these beverages. Consumers rely upon such claims when deciding to purchase such products," the lawsuit says

"The 21 grams of sugar contained in a venti Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha is roughly equal to five teaspoons of sugar. This is almost as much total sugar as is contained in a standard Kit Kat bar."
A screen grab of an Instagram post by Starbucks from Oct. 23, 2025, that advertises some protein beverages as sugar-free. (@Starbucks/Instagram)
A spokesperson for Starbucks told CBC News Wednesday they believe the lawsuit's claims have "no merit."

"Starbucks has consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices and nutritional content ... and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves," the spokesperson said.

items: Soon, even your Starbucks latte can come with protein. Is the trend healthy, or just big business?

blocks.text: So, are the drinks sugar-free, or not? Is the labelling misleading? And is it just U.S. drinks, or Canada, too?
Let's take a closer look at the lawsuit and what we know.
What are the drinks in question?
The lawsuit lists eight protein beverages that Starbucks labels as sugar-free:

items: Sugar-free vanilla protein latte.
Sugar-free caramel protein latte.
Sugar-free vanilla protein matcha.
Sugar-free caramel protein matcha.
Iced sugar-free vanilla protein latte.
Iced sugar-free caramel protein latte.
Iced sugar-free vanilla protein matcha.
Iced sugar-free caramel protein matcha.

blocks.text: Each item is available on both U.S. and Starbucks Canada websites under "protein beverages." And while the eight drinks are listed under a "no added sugar options" heading, each beverage currently has "sugar-free" in its title.

Starbucks launched the beverages in September 2025, citing statistics claiming that "71 per cent of Canadian consumers want to eat more protein." In a news release at the time, Starbucks noted its new protein drinks will be "available unsweetened or sugar-free and are designed to support customers looking to add protein to their order."
Coffee chains look to cash in on protein’s popularity
Are they sugar-free, or not?

No, each beverage contains sugar — anywhere between 13 and 21 grams per venti-size serving. At the higher end, that's about equivalent to the grams of sugar in a KitKat or Coffee Crisp chocolate bar, according to Health Canada.

When you click through the individual drinks on the company website, Starbucks lists nutritional information for each "sugar-free" protein beverage, including the grams of sugar by size. A venti iced sugar-free vanilla protein latte, for instance, is listed as containing 13 grams of sugar, and a venti sugar-free caramel protein matcha has 21 grams of sugar.
As the lawsuit points out, "the sugar-free products all contain milk, which contains lactose, a naturally occurring sugar."

items: Whey up: Protein powder prices soar as global demand grows
Is it unprofessional to bring iced coffee to a job interview? Gen Z is being dragged for it

blocks.text: If it's natural sugar, what's the issue?
The issue isn't where the sugar comes from, but the sugar-free labelling, the lawsuit argues.

"Despite knowing that Sugar-Free products contain milk, and knowing that this milk contains lactose, and knowing that this lactose is a sugar, and despite actually classifying this lactose as a sugar, Starbucks nonetheless calls these beverages 'Sugar-Free,'" the lawsuit says.
"Starbucks calls these beverages 'Sugar-Free' because it knows that consumers rely on such representations when deciding what products to purchase."
What are the consumer protection laws?
U.S. federal law prohibits Starbucks from using "sugar-free" to describe beverages containing more than 0.5 grams of sugar per 12-ounce serving, the complaint said. Even if the sugar comes from milk.

Similarly, in Canada, for something to be labelled as sugar-free, the food must contain less than 0.5 grams of sugars per reference amount and serving of stated size, according to the Food and Drug Regulations.
Are the new labels on high fat, sugar and sodium foods visible enough?

In both countries, there's a difference between labelling something as "sugar-free," like Starbucks has done with the protein drink names, or as having "no added sugars," which is how Starbucks also describes the drinks in the nutritional information because it uses sugar-free syrups.
Lactose is listed as a sugar in both Canada and the U.S.

Food producers are regularly sued for alleged false advertising, including in dozens of recent cases challenging "sugar-free" or "zero sugar" claims for products containing a sugar substitute known as allulose.
What happens next?

The complaint seeks unspecified damages for false advertising and violations of various state consumer protection laws. It also seeks to have the lawsuit certified as a class action and demands a trial by jury "on all issues so triable."
The lawsuit was filed on behalf of three individual consumers who bought Starbucks's sugar-free protein drinks in California, New York and Washington.

Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, including health-related issues such as diabetes, Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of the Seattle-headquartered firm that filed the lawsuit, said in a news release.
"And for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant," Berman said.
“Beverages with this much sugar are like drinking a candy bar.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: As US midterm elections loom, Trump's campaign tactics are becoming increasingly unusual, and expensive
articles.summary: Despite not being on the ballot, Trump is campaigning hard ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. His tactics and promises have mostly been at the expense of US taypayers. Experts say some might…

image.caption: Donald Trump has been campaigning to retain a Republican majority in the upcoming midterm electionsImage: Kent Nishimura/AFP

blocks.text: It's neither a joke nor fake news but a real report from earlier this week: Donald Trump has backed down. On Monday, the US president announced that a series of advertisements aired in September promoting him and his administration would no longer be funded with taxpayer money.

"The radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our great USA, and paying for them with USA money," Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.
He went on to claim that funding partisan ads with public money was a "rather standard thing to do," before adding that future ads would be paid with money raised from donations.

The ads themselves have caused some controversy in the United States. They ran in September between popular shows such as Saturday Night Live and football games, marked with the line: "paid for by the US government" — that is, paid with tax dollars.

The commercials showed scenes such as when US troops captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year but they mostly consisted of images and videos of Trump himself, along with combative messages that he would "expel the warmongers" or "throw off the sick political class," and ensure that the US did not become a communist state.
Why Europe's far right is turning away from Trump
Public funds for personal praise

Political opponents and a series of NGOs responded to the campaign with sharp criticism. Not only does US law prohibit the use of taypayer funds for political advertisements, but the ads also appeared shortly before the midterms — elections held near the midpoint of a president's four-year term.

On Tuesday, the US broadcasting network CBS reported that, according to contracting records, the US Department of Homeland Security had paid an agency $20 million (€17.9 million) for a "national media campaign."

The "rather standard" practice that Trump referred to actually applies to public service announcements, but this is not what the campaign ads are, argued the US non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

"Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising," the organization wrote in a public complaint to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ."Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump's recent campaign ads."

Independent experts have also voiced concerns. Patrick Malone, a professor in the department of Public Administration and Policy at American University in Washington DC, said the timing of the videos was problematic.

"You're not supposed to use taxpayer dollars to pay for anything that's campaign-related," he told DW. "Technically, [Trump] is not campaigning. He's not saying 'Vote for me!' The thing that's created the challenge here is the timing. Weeks before the midterms, this is a real big issue."
US Iran attack launched without US Congress, UN approval
Will the Republicans keep their majority after midterms?

Voters do not choose presidents in the midterm elections but members of Congres, which comprises the Senate and the House of Representatives and is the legislative branch of the federal government. On November 3, those eligible to vote will cast their ballots for all the seats in the House of Representatives, and roughly a third of the seats in the Senate. Some states will also be choosing governors.

Republicans have not been faring well in recent polls, which may be why Trump has been trying to promote his party's achievements. The Republicans currently hold a majority in both houses, with 53 of 100 seats in the Senate, and 219 of 435 seats in the House of Representatives. This has enabled Trump to pass a large number of his proposals fairly easily.

But a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday indicates that this could soon change. "Voters age 50 or older preferred Trump's party over the Democratic Party by just 2 percentage points — 44% to 42% — compared to an 8-point Republican advantage in December," it found. This age bracket "is particularly important for midterm elections, when older Americans historically have made up large shares of the electorate."
Meanwhile, among voters under the age of 50, "Democrats led by 18 points," the survey showed.

The poll also found that opinions on Trump himself were low, with "32% of Americans giving a thumbs up to Trump's presidency." This level of approval, the study highlighted, was unchanged from an earlier poll "that saw the leader's rating at the lowest of his political career."
Republicans shy away from Trump's support
This could also be one of the reasons why Republican candidates do not seem so keen on making public appearances with the president, usually a highlight of a campaign trail.
Many US citizens associate Trump with high living costs, or the war with Iran, which has dragged on for over half a year now.

One Republican operative told the news website Politico on condition of anonymity that if the the president were to visit a battleground state — where Democratic and Republican support is fairly equal among voters — to campaign for his party, they suspected their "candidates would come down with COVID" to avoid having to attend.

In September, a number of Republicans skipped Trump's big party convention — typically reserved for presidential, not midterm elections — even though the event could have offered them a platform for their campaign.

Susan Collins from Maine and Dan Sullivan from Alaska, are just two examples of Republican senators whose seats are on the line and who did not attend. Neither did candidates for the House of Representatives from the swing states Arizona, Iowa and Michigan.
Trump offers Americans $5,000 for midterm victory
Trump promises $5,000 payout if Republicans win
Those who skipped the event missed the president repeating an unusual campaign message: To encourage more people to vote, Trump urged supporters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.
And if that wasn't enough, he also promised each US citizen eligible to vote a $5,000 payout if Republicans maintained their majority in both houses of Congress.
Keeping that pledge could cost the federal government over $1.2 trillion, but observers doubt it would ever come to that.

"He has no money to do that with. It would have to be authorized and appropriated by Congress," Mallone explained. "I think the likelihood is very slim," he added. "It's one of those things like 'Mexico is going to pay for the wall.'"
Whether Trump's commercials or promised payouts will be enough to rally majority Republican support remains to be seen.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen
articles.summary:
Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land

Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen,…

blocks.text: Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen, approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.

The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador to Yemen, Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.

Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west.

blocks.caption: A Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter is seen purportedly firing at a Houthi position near Dhubab in Taiz. Photograph: Southern Giants Brigades/Reuters

blocks.text: Houthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded.

The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that the Houthis have stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”.
There has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims about Yemeni government advances issued at the beginning of the week.

Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people.

The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel.

Southern Giant forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. Their forces are now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait.

articles.title: NASA's Curiosity rover takes striking image of dawn on Mars
articles.summary: NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing ‌jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues…

image.caption: A view of the Martian surface taken by NASA's Curiosity rover on Aug. 11. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/Reuters)

blocks.text: Science·New

NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing ‌jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth's planetary neighbour.
Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator
Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a five-kilometre-tall mountain rising from the crater floor.
The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover's Mastcam camera about ​an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved ​cliffs in the distance.

"The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far," said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist.

NASA believes that some kind of wind-blown sediment landed in the crater from nearby volcanic activity. Once it hardened into rock, "eons of wind carved ‌up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs," Vasvada said.

The yardang layer most likely formed about three billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 16 ⁠kilometres across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp.
But the layers appears to have been added on later, he said.
"It's above what geologists call an ‌unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top."
Rover making gradual ascent up mountain
The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of nearly a kilometre in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars, according to NASA.

Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a ​period of the planet's geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have learned more about bodies of water — lakes and streams — that long ago covered this region, at ⁠a time when Mars was wetter and warmer than the cold and desolate place it is today.

items: NASA rover adds to growing list of organic compounds detected on Mars
Mars rover snaps pictures of giant, dark sand dunes

blocks.text: Vasavada said NASA hopes ⁠Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at which time it will use its instruments to ⁠scrutinize ⁠the geology there.

Curiosity has been studying the ​geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harboring microbial life. It is one of two ​NASA rovers operating on Mars. The ⁠Perseverance rover is currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere.
Curiosity's new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly.
"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky," Vasavada said.
"But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades ⁠of blue. It's like Earth, but ‌it's definitely Mars."

articles.title: Canada to extend assisted dying exclusion for people whose sole condition is mental illness
articles.summary:
Legislation an effort by ruling Liberals to address growing clash over who has access to doctor-assisted death

Canada’s federal government said Wednesday it would advance legislation to…

blocks.text: Canada’s federal government said Wednesday it would advance legislation to prevent people whose sole health condition is mental illness from accessing euthanasia, an effort by the ruling Liberal party to address a clash in the country over who has access to physician-assisted death.

Under the current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessing medical assistance in dying (Maid) to end their lives. But that ban – due to be lifted in March – has divided lawmakers over whether to permit this expansion of the Maid program.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the justice minister, Sean Fraser, said his government would indefinitely bar people whose sole condition is mental illness from accessing the program. He said that while there was no “perfect consensus” on this issue, upcoming legislation reflected the “correct” approach.

Earlier this year, a government committee concluded the government should expand access to Maid and should “indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness from eligibility for medical assistance in dying”. That report also flagged the need for “increased and more equitable access” to mental health services.

Canada’s medical assistance in dying (Maid) laws, drawn up after a 2015 supreme court decision, initially only permitted those who are terminally ill to be eligible for the procedure. But in 2019, a Quebec judge ruled that restricting access to those who had a “reasonably foreseeable death” was unconstitutional, forcing federal lawmakers to amend and expand the existing laws.

In 2021, the law was updated so adults could receive an assisted death if two doctors confirmed an irremediable physical condition causing immense suffering that cannot be relieved. Given the uncertainty surrounding mental illness, lawmakers in 2021 initially put a temporary exclusion in place for people who suffer solely from a mental illness. They renewed that pause in 2023 and 2024.

According to the latest government figures, the vast majority of Maid deaths – 95.6% – involved people whose natural death was considered “reasonably foreseeable”. Only 4.4% were cases in which death was not considered reasonably foreseeable. Those include people with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and incurable neurological disease that can causes profound disability and immense suffering.

The Liberal party’s legislation is also an effort to ward off a private member’s bill that would amend the section of the criminal code covering Maid so that “a mental disorder is not a grievous and irremediable medical condition”.

Advocates for expanding Maid to include mental illness alone say the current rules violate their constitutional rights and access to healthcare. Fraser acknowledged to reporters that a federal case, led by the advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada, to challenge the government’s previous decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness, could affect the upcoming bill.

Fraser said lawmakers would also work to decriminalize what are known as advanced requests, effectively giving people suffering from some illnesses such as Alzheimer’s the chance to choose Maid before their illness deprives them of the capacity to consent.

At present, Quebec is the only jurisdiction that permits the use of these requests. Fraser gave no specifics on the timing of the legislation but said that provinces will decide whether to provide advance requests. While the province of Alberta has already said it will not permit advance requests, the jusice minister said the bill attempts to ensure “the doctors who provide the services will not be treated as criminals for doing so”.
