articles.title: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil
articles.summary: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian rule
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, fuelling fears over a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power.
Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president, Jair Bolsonaro, has long praised.

Last year, Jair Bolsonaro, a former soldier who served under that military regime, was jailed for 27 years for trying to engineer a coup after he lost the 2022 election to the current leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

But Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the 25 October run-off as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”.
“The only thing standing in the way of Brazil becoming a barbarity is called Flávio Bolsonaro as president,” he claimed at a campaign event in Goiânia, a city near the capital, Brasília.

The incendiary comments caused outrage among historians and opponents of Bolsonaro’s radical populist movement, who have accused him of co-opting the language of democracy to disguise an illiberal shift.

blocks.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro raises hands with former presidential candidate Ronaldo Caiado (left) and Sao Paulo governor Tarcisio de Freitas during a rally in Goiania, Goias state, Brazil. Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Talíria Petrone, the leftwing congresswoman, wrote on X: “This is the announcement of a coup.”

Marcelo Freixo, a newly elected congressman from Lula’s Workers’ party (PT), said: “Brazil was re-democratised in 1988. The person who tried to undo this was his father, who was convicted of an attempted coup. What they want, once again, is a coup.”

Bolsonaro did not spell out what he meant by “re-democratising” Brazil, a vibrant if polarised multi-party democracy which the Sweden based V-Dem institute ranks 28th on its liberal democracy index, two places ahead of the UK and 23 ahead of the US.
But Jair Bolsonaro, who has praised authoritarian leaders including Chile’s former dictator Augusto Pinochet, has long hankered for a return to military rule.

Last September, the supreme court found Jair Bolsonaro guilty of trying to convince military chiefs to help him cling to power at the end of his 2018-2022 presidency. The conspiracy culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, a far-right insurrection seemingly inspired by the January 6 storming of the US Capitol.

Writing in the O Globo newspaper, Míriam Leitão, a prominent political and economic journalist, warned that, if Bolsonaro won, Brazil faced “the extreme and concrete danger of … another coup d’état attempt”.
“Flávio follows the same ideas as his father and has already said that an intervention in the institutions is necessary,” Leitão wrote.

“If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, he will have more tools at his disposal to carry out his father’s authoritarian project: robust caucuses in the lower house and senate, a weakened supreme court, and the support of the Donald Trump administration. Political science shows that it’s in the second term that an autocrat doubles down on their plan. Look at the case of Donald Trump. The risk isn’t of the son repeating the father, it’s that he surpasses him,” Leitão said.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro flash victory signs during a rally ahead of the presidential election runoff. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters

blocks.text: Political scientist Miguel Lago said Sunday’s far-right election triumph – in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) secured the senate’s largest caucus, with 28 of its 81 seats – would permit radical changes, including the impeachment of supreme court ministers considered enemies of the Bolsonarismo movement.

Jair Bolsonaro and his jailed co-conspirators are also likely to be freed if his son wins, with the former president expected to become an influential minister able to select the new heads of the armed forces.
“It’s better than a coup d’état … it’s almost like a coup d’état with the support of the majority of the population,” Lago said.

Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, has been accused of “killing” democracy by using control over the country’s congress and institutions to approve sweeping constitutional changes, including scrapping presidential term limits so he can seek indefinite re-election.

Flávio Bolsonaro recently met Bukele’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, in São Paulo, hailing the Central American country’s hardline security policies, which have seen thousands jailed during a state of exception that has lasted nearly five years. Bolsonaro told reporters that during their conversation, Villatoro “stressed the importance” of using control of congress to make the “necessary legal changes”.

On Tuesday, the president of Bolsonaro’s party, Valdemar Costa Neto, said that if Flávio Bolsonaro became president, he would release his father, who would then be “a strong candidate” in the 2030 presidential election.

articles.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors
articles.summary: Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London
articles.byline: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem

blocks.text: The UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs that it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.

The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.
The forced closure marked the lowest point in UK-Israeli relations for decades, with reports of the UK considering a retaliatory expulsion of 27 Israeli diplomats from London.

It would be the Palestinians who pay the price for the consulate’s closing, warned Amjad Iraqi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst on Israel and Palestine. The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv – which remains open – and provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, services they will now lose.

“It’s quite telling that the Israeli government response was primarily about blocking the UK’s ability to support Palestinians, rather than the core of UK-Israeli relations themselves,” Iraqi said. “For [the Israeli] foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, the response is low-cost, in their minds it’s just Palestinians bearing the cost.”
Israel has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of countries like the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinian residents of Sheikh Jarrah, the East Jerusalem neighbourhood that is home to the consulate, appeared resigned when asked about the impact the closure might have on their lives.

“I mean, it was the British that were the basis of the issue wasn’t it? They were the ones who signed the Balfour declaration?” said Abu Abdo, a 79-year-old former repairman and resident of Sheikh Jarrah, referring to a 1917 document by the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour, which expressed support for a Jewish state in Palestine.
It was a dramatic end for the consulate’s tenure in East Jerusalem, which since its move to the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in 1967, had seen its fair share of political upheaval.

The UK government first bought the plot that would become its consulate in 1963, when East Jerusalem was still under Jordanian control. It was meant to be a direct liaison between the UK government and the Jordanian-administered West Bank and East Jerusalem. The compound took four years to build and was finally ready for the UK consul-general to move into by 1967.

But by the time the consul moved into, however, East Jerusalem was no longer under the control of the Jordanians. Just weeks before the new consul-general, John Henry Lewen, was to move into the building, the six-day war broke out, and Israel captured East Jerusalem from the Jordanian forces.

Lewen assumed his post at the present day consulate in a changed East Jerusalem under Israeli control. The consulate he oversaw occupied a unique position, as the UK did not recognise Jerusalem as being under any single country’s control.

As the UK foreign secretary told parliament in June 1967: “Our consul-general in Jerusalem is subordinate neither to the ambassador in Tel Aviv nor to the ambassador in Amman, but directly to the Foreign Office.”

Lewen’s tenure was marked by the political problems that plagued Jerusalem in the aftermath of the six-day war, and the birth of Israel. In 1969, a bomb was placed under the window of a consul secretary, harming no one but damaging the compound.
Years later, Palestinians would present their grievances to the British consulate in Sheikh Jarrah.

In 2017, protesters demonstrated outside the consulate to mark the centenary of the Balfour declaration. Men placed flags in the consululate windows reading “Balfour is a crime”, while schoolgirls carried thousands of letters written by Palestinian students asking Britain to apologise for the declaration.

This week, however, there was little sign of the political turmoil which the British consulate had waded through during its 60-years on the site. The neighbourhood, mostly made up of diplomatic missions and UN and other international organisations’ offices, was quiet.
Residents in the area expressed disappointment over what they saw as a lack of international support for the Palestinian people in recent years.
“We have seen very little but studies and words, no action from the international community,” said Abu Abdo.

articles.title: South Sudan's road to elections remains uncertain
articles.summary: South Sudan's first general election is set for December 22. Insecurity, political tensions and failure to begin voter registration have raised doubts over whether the poll can be held credibly.
articles.byline: James Shimanyula, Eddy Micah Jr., Isaac Mugabi, Isaac Kaledzi

image.caption: South Sudan's President Salva Kiir is set to contest in the December electionImage: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Sudan has scheduled a general election for December 22. It will be the first since the country gained independence from Sudan in 2011.

But political tensions are high as preparations lag. Debate over the election intensified after President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on September 22 to form a caretaker administration.
Some voters are skeptical that the election will take place
Many are worried not only about the electoral logistics and insecurity in the country known for violent power struggles and political instability, according to Denis Logonyi, a Juba-based journalist.
Will elections happen in South Sudan?
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

"People are having different views on these elections," Logonyi told DW. "You hear discussions in political circles and on social media, but ordinary people are not talking much about elections," Logonyi told DW.
"There has been no voter education, no voter registration, and only a few months remain," one voter said.
Another voter told DW that while South Sudanese are eager for a credible election process, the country was not adequately prepared.
Food prices are rising, civil servants are not being paid, and displaced people are struggling, the voter said.
Politicians admit to 'obstacles' but agree to adhere to election timeline
Political parties have until October 22 to present their manifestos and register.
On October 7, South Sudan concluded a two-week Inter-Party Dialogue. Thirty-nine parties took part in discussions on the critical issues ahead of the election.
The meeting was initiated by Kiir, with some civil society groups left out, according to Logonyi. Minister of Cabinet Affairs Dr. Martin Elia Lomuro outlined a few of the challenges.

"Delayed funding could severely affect civic education and election infrastructure. There is need for a clear legal framework to govern the participation of the country's administrative areas. The three administrative areas are not clearly reflected in the National Election Act, which is necessary for the election outcomes to be accepted," Lomuro said.

"A credible election requires security readiness throughout the entire cycle — including campaign rallies, polling stations, voting, counting, and results transmission. The unified security forces have not yet been fully deployed."

According to Albino Akol Atak, the Deputy Rapporteur of the Inter-Party Dialogue and Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the parties unanimously agreed to adhere to the election timeline.
"The election train has left the station, and it has no reverse gear. We are trying to smooth the pathway for this train to arrive on December 22, 2026, without obstacles," Atak said.
Meanwhile, Changkuoth Bichok Reath, Secretary General of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), said the success of the election would depend entirely on urgent, comprehensive collaboration.

"The South Sudan Opposition Alliance strongly believes that successfully conducting the election on December 22 requires coordinated, inclusive action from all national institutions, political parties, security actors, civil society, and other stakeholders," Reath said.

"Given the limited time remaining, priority should be placed on resolving outstanding legal issues and ensuring constructive dialogue among political actors. Furthermore, political parties must be funded to meet key requirements, because a lack of funding will only draw us backward."
Sudan has a history of planning then postponing elections
South Sudan has endured decades of conflict, from long wars that preceded independence to a devastating civil war that erupted just two years after it became a sovereign state.

Power-sharing transitional governments have been in place under fragile peace deals — including the Revitalized Peace Agreement of September 2018. Elections have repeatedly been planned then put off since.
Armed opposition groups remain active, and many citizens fear political tensions could trigger renewed violence.
"The absence of Riek Machar from the political process is a major concern," Logonyi said. "If there is to be an election or a meaningful political dialogue, many believe he has to be part of it."

The 2018 power-sharing deal that saw Kiir become president and Machar — his long-time rival and main opposition leader — vice president briefly stabilized the country. However, tensions between the two persisted.
In March 2025, Machar was placed under house arrest and later put on trial for offences that include treason and murder.

blocks.caption: South Sudan's former Vice President Riek Machar pictured in court in Juba in September 2025Image: Peter Louis Gume/AFP

blocks.text: Key conditions envisioned for elections under peace deal not fulfilled yet

"The government has demonstrated that it is keen for the election to happen," said Wambui Njehu Nzigo, an analyst with Control Risks. "But there are important processes that have not yet taken place."

The lack of voter registration is among the biggest concerns. "If elections are to take place soon, you would expect there already to be a voter register," Nzigo said. "There is very little time for that to happen."
Security reforms required under the 2018 peace deal are unfinished. These include the unification of armed groups to create the conditions for a stable transition.
Analysts have long been warning that the legitimacy of any election without these key issues being addressed would be undermined.

"The elections would be taking place in an environment where there is still active fighting in some parts of the country," Nzigo said. "The fact that the main opposition leader is under house arrest raises questions about whether this will be a true competition."
According to Logonyi, civil society groups are calling for greater dialogue, political inclusion and protections for journalists and activists before the vote is held.
How instability persists in South Sudan
Ongoing flooding could interfere with the vote
South Sudan is facing severe flooding, displacement and food insecurity. These conditions could make it difficult for some citizens to reach polling stations, Nzigo said.
For communities displaced by conflicts in particular, there's uncertainty over how they would register and cast their ballots.
Floodwaters, oil and health fears in South Sudan
Experts warn that a vote without broad participation could lead to a disputed outcome and instensify conflict.
Regional organizations such as the African Union and international partners are expected to continue encouraging an inclusive political process.
Analysts argue that the focus should be not only on ensuring elections take place, but also on creating conditions that make them credible.
For many South Sudanese, the choice is clear: elections alone won't guarantee stability.

articles.title: China's Golden Week reveals cautious consumer spending despite travel surge
articles.summary: Chinese visitors are returning from trips after the 13-day Golden Week holiday. Their subdued spending has raised fresh questions about domestic demand in the world's second-largest economy.

image.caption: Golden Week is typically a time of high levels of travel and spending in ChinaImage: Ryohei Moriya/The Yomiuri Shimbun/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ya Xi just returned to Shanghai on a red-eye flight after her Golden Week trip to Southeast Asia. "I can stay up all night for a cheaper ticket," she told DW.
She was among the 31.19 million passengers who traveled during the 13-day holiday period that followed the Mid-Autumn Festival on September 25 and China's National Day on October 1.
Many of them spent their budgets more cautiously this year.

"I earn less this year, so I'm lowering my budget for this year's Golden Week," said Xi, who is in her mid-20s. "I spent 5,000 yuan (about €660) on my flight, which was the largest expense of my trip."

Golden Week is viewed as a barometer of the Chinese economy with Beijing using it as an opportunity to showcase the world's second-largest economy's spending power. State media, for instance, reported a record-breaking 25.204 million passenger trips on China's railway network on October 1.

blocks.caption: State media reported record-breaking train passenger numbers over Golden WeekImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, early data indicated more moderate spending per traveler and broadly flat passenger traffic, according to Citigroup analysts. Traffic volume during the first four days of the holiday rose just 0.1% year over year, far below the 3.5% increase seen during this year's Labor Day vacation.
Selective spending among younger consumers
Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese Economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told DW that Chinese consumers are becoming increasingly selective.
"My read is that people are willing to get out and spend. They're just being much more careful about how much and what they spend on," Lee said.

But being cautious doesn't mean staying frozen, she added. "They'll spend on travel, concerts, restaurants, experiences, and tech… if they think it's worth it, they'll economize pretty aggressively elsewhere."

Xi's Golden Week trip followed this pattern, paying more for significant experiences and economizing elsewhere: "Eat, drink, and be merry," said Xi, indicating she was willing to spend more on food. For example, she set a 200-yuan (about €26) budget for each meal.

blocks.caption: Many Chinese are opting for budget travel options instead of luxury tripsImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: Guo-Chen Wang, an associate research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, told DW that the budget-travel trend among Chinese visitors was ongoing.
"The number of trips is increasing, butconsumption remains strained, as I saw in past years," Wang said.

The Chinese government attempted to boost Golden Week spending by providing coupons worth more than 310 million yuan (€41.2 million). Wang remained unconvinced about the effectiveness of such a measure: "That's an old solution to an old problem."
A sign of China's weak domestic demand

It isn't the first Golden Week to see weak consumer demand. During last year's holiday season, the average spending per trip was 911.04 yuan (around €121), the lowest in three years, according to Reuters.
"Beijing still believes the low spending was due to consumers' reluctance [to spend]," Wang said. "In fact, we think Chinese consumers are unable to spend."

While savings kept increasing in Chinese banks, Wang said the vast majority of the savings are held by a small proportion of the population. "In other words, the majority of Chinese people don't have savings."
"The fundamental issue is the wealth gap in Chinese society," he said. "I don't know whether Beijing really neglected this problem or was simply unwilling to face it."
China’s tourism surge: expansion, regulation and challenges

A recent International Monetary Fund publication, Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China, once again noted that China's domestic demand has been weak since the pandemic, when the property market correction began.
Lee, however, saw weak spending during this Golden Week as a confidence problem.

"Theproperty downturnhas hit household wealth, income and job expectations are still pretty soft, and several years of weak prices have trained people to wait for discounts and hunt for value," she told DW.
Tightened cross-border rules played a limited role

Weeks before the Golden Week, China's tightened travel restrictions took effect on September 15. The new restrictions ban citizens from leaving the country if they are deemed to pose a risk to national as well as industrial or technological security.

Wang expected Chinese tourists to turn to domestic travel under the new rules, but the outcome did not match his expectations. "The volume of travel abroad is in fact growing, though not by much," he said.
Lee said she saw little evidence of a broad chilling effect on ordinary outbound tourism, with the Golden Week numbers serving as a "useful reality check."
"The September rules give authorities more room to verify travel purposes and ask for additional information in some cases," Lee said. "They still leave plenty of room for ordinary overseas tourism."
Mi Tang in Taipei contributed to this article.

articles.title: German spy scandal threatens national security
articles.summary: The arrest of Germany's former intelligence chief August Hanning could undermine national security, experts warn, as allies may reconsider their intelligence relationships.

image.caption: The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationshipsImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D.*, is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.

Manfred D. is accused of having sold around 2,000 highly classified documents to Hanning over a period of 12 years, long after the latter stepped down from the BND in 2005, after seven years as its chief. Manfred D. continued to serve all of Hanning's successors, including the current BND chief Martin Jäger, before retiring in March this year.
On one occasion, the state prosecutor said, Hanning "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service."
DW's Michaela Küfner looks at Germany's espionage scandal

According to Florian Flade, reporter for public broadcaster ARD, most of these documents were weekly intelligence briefings delivered to the German government by the BND, including the latest findings from partner intelligence agencies in other countries.

"This is very, very sensitive because it involves partner agencies in other countries," Flade told DW's Berlin Briefing podcast. "And we heard this also involves information about the Iranian nuclear program, the Russian military, also the Ukraine war."
Broken trust, broken credibility

Some pundits now say that the biggest concern is what conclusions the intelligence agencies of allied countries will draw from this affair. In the past, the US CIA is known to have shared information on radical Islamists in Germany, which possibly helped to prevent terrorist attacks in the country.

If it now emerges that information was leaving the BND via Hanning, that relationship could be undermined, particularly if it was also eventually ending up in the hands of the intelligence agencies of Russia and China (though there is no suggestion of that as yet).

"There's huge damage being done not only to the outer appearance and image of the BND," said Flade. "There's a damage assessment now happening within the BND. Also, they're talking to partners about this because they want to know if their information was given to other countries."

That could also potentially have consequences for Germany's national security in the growing confrontation with Russia. The BND, which is currently subject to more legal restrictions than other intelligence agencies around the world, considers its relationship with its US counterpart as vital.

"There might be a change in the amount of information that is coming from the US and others," Flade added, though ultimately, he pointed out, it might be difficult for the BND to know what they're not being told.
Security loopholes in Germany's parliament spark concern

Only a day before the scandal broke, current BND President Martin Jäger reiterated his concern that Germany could slide into a military conflict with Russia, telling a parliamentary hearing that the Kremlin was already waging a "shadow war," and that further military rearmament was "unfortunately necessary" — though he did say that there was currently no indication of active preparations from Russia.

Flade said that, behind the scenes, Jäger is furious about the leak of information from Manfred D., and called a meeting on Tuesday of all BND officials to underline the how serious the consequences of sharing information could be. New internal security measures are also being put in place.

The new case could not have come at a worse time for Jäger or the BND. For one thing, new laws are currently being prepared to expand the agency's powers, partly to improve the BND's standing among its foreign partners.

For another thing, another BND agent, Carsten L. and a businessman named Arthur E., are currently on trial in Berlin on treason charges for passing on classified documents to the Russian secret service in 2022.

blocks.caption: Florian Flade is an espionage expert and guest in DW's Berlin Briefing podcast this weekImage: DW

blocks.text: New rules for old officials?

The case has also raised questions about what former intelligence officials should and shouldn't be allowed to do once they leave office. Hanning founded his own security consultancy business after he left the BND, for which he apparently used his contacts and knowledge to advise his clients. This is legal and tolerated, but many think it shouldn't be.

Timo Lange, of the NGO LobbyControl, said that the Hanning case shows why former intelligence officials must be prevented from working as security consultants in any capacity for the rest of their lives.

"It is fundamentally problematic when high-ranking officials from the intelligence or military sectors, after leaving government service, act as consultants for various — and in some cases unknown — clients from abroad," Lange said in a statement. "This is an obvious gateway for illegitimate foreign influence and jeopardizes the security interests of Germany and the European Union."

But as Flade pointed out, Hanning's career path is not exactly unusual. "These people are trying to just make some money with what they can do best, which is networking and then selling the security assessments that they do," he said. "And yeah, working for companies or even for other countries as a consultant."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners
articles.summary:
Inquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not lead to success at polls

More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important…

blocks.text: More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.
This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.

The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%.

The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%. But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won.

blocks.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro has shown he is as willing as his father, Jair, to curb nature protections and allow Indigenous territories to be exploited. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees.

If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration.

Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest.

blocks.caption: Lula’s social media campaign has not been as effective as that of the Bolsonaro team.  Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: He is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará, Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (692 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs.

Bolsonarist influence in the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Jair’s brother, Eduardo, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies. Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff.

blocks.caption: A Flavio Bolsonaro supporter rides in a truck decorated with campaign stickers for the far-right presidential candidate at a rally in Goiania, Goias state. Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: As a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns.

That inquest is already under way. Many focus on the influence of social media, which has been used far more effectively by the far right. During the Bolsonaro administration, his sons were part of the “hate cabinet” that spread fear and disinformation via WhatsApp groups and other online channels – Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos, was indicted by federal police for leading the group. Environmentalists were often the target.

Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife.

Lula, 80, has been slow to adapt. Although he is arguably the most iconic and successful Latin American politician of the 21st century, his messaging seems less attuned to the people than it was in his heyday. The Workers party has struggled in an era of weaker unions and in some ways been the victim of its own success – with education and social policies that raised millions out of poverty and created greater expectations for consumption and entrepreneurism; and huge subsidies to farmers, who now support the right wing because they chaff at environmental limits.

blocks.caption: A woman looks at posters depicting the former president Jair Bolsonaro, alongside the words: ‘Remember that?’ Photograph: Pilar Olivares/Reuters

blocks.text: Tied into those explanations are the geopolitics of the climate and nature crisis, which is exacerbating great power rivalry between the US and China and amplifying extreme ideologies as much as extreme weather. In this light, the Brazil election is just the latest in a broader pattern of the far right taking control to expand extractivism despite growing evidence that the capitalist economy is breaking planetary boundaries. In the past two years, Donald Trump has ripped apart environmental regulations in the US and treated the rest of the Americas as his sphere of influence. Argentina was already onboard. Venezuela has been invaded for its resources, while in Colombia, Peru and Chile there has been a sharp shift to the right.

Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. His son Eduardo urged the US to apply tariffs on Brazilian people to “punish” the government for imprisoning his father. The Brazilian intelligence agency has warned that the US was trying to interfere in the election.

That election isn’t over yet. Lula stands a small chance if he can win over the many millions of voters who chose not to mark their ballots for either candidate. But the odds are stacked against him. Most of the eliminated candidates were on the right so their supporters are more likely to switch to Bolsonaro. No first round leader has ever failed to win the runoff of a Brazilian presidential election.

Voters, of course, are allowed to change their minds. Either on 25 October or, constitutionally, in four years’ time. But for how much longer will that be possible? If Bolsonaro wins, it won’t just be Lula that is finished, it could also be the Amazon and democracy itself.

articles.title: Germany: Did CDU lawmakers support the far-right AfD?
articles.summary: Lawmakers of the center-right CDU may have voted for the far-right AfD candidate for parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt. Germany's Social Democrats warn of a "unique breach of taboos."

image.caption: The election of the first parliamentary speaker of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, triggered SPD protests in BerlinImage: Jens Krick/Flashpic/picture alliance

blocks.text: Following events in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday, speculation is rife that lawmakers from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) helped elect a far-right extremist as parliamentary speaker, in violation not only of prior internal agreements, but also despite the insistence of CDU Chairman, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, that his party would not cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) anywhere.

In the first session of the parliament in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, following the AfD's election victory on September 6, Tobias Rausch was elected parliamentary speaker — the first time a representative of a far-right party had held such a position since the end of World War II.

Rausch was backed by his own party and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Rationality (BSW), formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance — as had been expected — but he also received four additional votes by secret ballot. Most observers believe these votes could only have come from right-wing CDU lawmakers.
Far-right AfD wins first state parliament speaker post

Leading members of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) were quick to take to the streets in protest in Berlin on Tuesday, marching from the Bundestag through the Brandenburg Gate to nearby Bebelplatz — the very spot where, in 1933, the Nazis burned books by authors they deemed unacceptable. The march concluded with SPD Federal Minister of Defense Boris Pistorius leading the crowd in the German national anthem, while many participants displayed copies of the German Basic Law, a symbol of democracy to stand up for the rule of law and the constitution.

Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) summarized the situation: "Electing far-right extremists to such an office represents a taboo brake. Not only the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could have happened." Klingbeil's SPD is, after all, the junior coalition partner in the federal government. The events in Magdeburg thus also cast a shadow over the governing coalition.
Did the AfD receive votes from the CDU?

It didn't help much that the leader of the CDU parliamentary group, Thorsten Frei, was careful in his wording: "It's a secret ballot, so of course, in principle, anybody is suspect." But he also added: "The fact that this happened is, in my view, extremely troubling and cause for concern."

The result of the first election in the new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt thus offers only a glimpse of the fierce debates to come on how to deal with the AfD. The far-right party won 44% of the vote after having campaigned on extremely tough immigration policies, climate change denial and calls for the near-total abolition of public broadcasting.

Despite its election victory, the AfD does not have a parliamentary majority of its own. In the small eastern state, the regional branch of the party has been classified by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution as "confirmed right-wing extremist."
Will CDU politicians help elect an AfD state premier into office?

So once again, the debate about the "firewall" returns. The term refers to the stance taken by democratic parties of ruling out any form of cooperation with the AfD. At the city and municipal levels, this approach has long since ceased to work.

Many political analysts have pointed out that the "firewall" has not benefited the CDU, but cooperating with the AfD is also seen as a slippery slope. Georg Maier, the SPD Interior Minister of the state of Thuringia, agrees: "If the CDU continues down this path, it will contribute to its own downfall. The firewall does serve a purpose."
Germany's great divide: Is Friedrich Merz losing the center?

BSW co-leader Fabio De Masi told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper: "We have to pull the AfD out from behind the firewall. Until now, it hasn't had to prove anything and has been able to conceal its internal contradictions. I don't want the AfD to continue growing behind the firewall."

The BSW, a party founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht that has retained some left-wing positions while also aligning itself with the AfD on social issues, paved the way for Rausch's election as parliamentary speaker when it announced that it would vote for him.
The BSW barely managed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. How closely its five MPs want to work with the AfD in the future remains to be seen.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?

AfD caucus leader Oliver Kirchner recently expressed criticism of BSW co-leaders De Masi and Mohamed Ali, who both have an immigrant background: "Am I now supposed to spend five years in politics with people who are under the leadership of Mohamed Ali and this half-Italian guy who says, 'They're all Nazis'?" Kirchner told the right-wing magazine Compact earlier this month.

Up until now, support from the BSW has been seen as the AfD's only real chance of coming to power in Saxony-Anhalt. The other parties — the CDU, the SPD, the Greens, and the Left Party — continue to categorically rule out any cooperation with the AfD. Whether that will remain the case in the coming weeks is now the big question.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?
articles.summary:
Lack of majority for Parti Québécois puts any referendum in doubt, especially amid bruising trade war with Trump

The victory of the Parti Québécois in Monday’s election in Quebec might seem…

blocks.text: The victory of the Parti Québécois in Monday’s election in Quebec might seem to bring its signature goal, of separating the French-speaking province from Canada, much closer – but Canadian unity may not be nearly as threatened as may first seem.

The PQ’s victory was both impressive and disappointing. The party added 56 seats to its roster and more than doubled its vote share compared to the 2022 election, giving it its first taste of power in 14 years. Crucially, however, it was left five seats short of a majority, making its promise to hold a referendum after Donald Trump leaves office in 2028 nearly impossible.
It also won with barely 28% of the popular vote, the lowest percentage for any government in Canada’s electoral history, according to the polling analyst Philippe Fournier.

The vast majority of Quebecers voted for parties that want nothing to do with a referendum. It’s a reflection of the province’s 30-year aversion to another bruising debate about Quebec’s place in Canada – particularly in the wake of Trump’s tariffs and threats against the country.

The result not only puts another referendum in doubt, but a raft of other PQ initiatives too, including abolishing the monarchy and applying Quebec’s strict language laws to the province’s colleges. The new government will also face stiff opposition to its plans to reduce immigration levels, which has angered farmers and the business community.

Meanwhile, the most popular politician in the province remains far and away the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, in large part because of his resistance to Trump. That has left PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon in an awkward situation for a separatist: he can’t be seen as a threat to Canadian unity. He essentially acknowledged this in his victory speech, pledging to be a “good-faith collaborator” with the rest of the country, and even addressing the crowd in English; then attempted to court the other side of the debate by announcing Tuesday he would prevent the lieutenant governor, who represents the British crown, from swearing in his new government.
“Seventy percent of Quebecers don’t want a referendum,” said John Parisella, who served as chief of staff to two Quebec premiers and the province’s delegate general in New York and Washington.

“And every time they see Trump’s picture on the screen at night, it does nothing to improve a desire for separation. For a lot of Quebecers, the link with Canada is absolutely crucial, even if it isn’t necessarily emotional.”

The vote, in fact, may have less to do with embracing separatism and more about punishing the current government. The election saw the total collapse of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which has been in power since 2018. An alliance of federalists and separatists (the party describes itself as nationalist), it didn’t win a single seat, and harvested just a third of its vote share compared to 2022. Its leader, Christine Fréchette, lost her own riding to the Parti Québécois, and on Tuesday afternoon she resigned.

In a province whose political discourse has focused on the federalist-separatist divide, the election also suggested a return to normalcy of sorts – with separatists returning to the PQ’s fold, while the federalist vote dispersed to the opposition Liberal party and the upstart Parti conservateur du Québec (PCQ).

The PCQ feasted on the CAQ’s support in the election, winning 19 ridings in the hinterland and in the Quebec City area, where leader Éric Duhaime won his seat for the first time. Founded in 2009, the populist party counts a prominent anti-vaxxer and a rage-bating anti-woke radio host as two of its winning candidates.

The party was able to break through in part because of its promise to build an underground highway linking Quebec City to its suburbs across the St Lawrence, despite government reports saying the endeavor would cost as much as C$9.3bn and do little to alleviate traffic.

Montreal, meanwhile, went decidedly Liberal red, with leader Charles Milliard regaining seats on the island and in the traditionally English redoubt of the Eastern Townships. The staunchly federalist Liberals, who are unaffiliated with Carney’s federal Liberals, will serve as Quebec’s official opposition. Governing with but a handful of seats in the province’s biggest metropolis will be challenging enough for the PQ; as history has shown, winning a referendum without it is somewhere near impossible.

Canada faces another potential menace to its sovereignty in a little less than two weeks, when Alberta in the west holds a “referendum on a referendum” on secession. Happily for Carney, and unfortunately for Trump, polls suggest Albertans are as averse to dalliances with separation as their Quebecois brethren have now become to the east – no matter the party they just chose to govern.

articles.title: Trump’s LA and San Diego comments ‘dangerous, if not treasonous’, says Newsom – US politics live
articles.summary: California governor critcizes president for ‘putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs’

blocks.text: Key events

items: 16m agoSusan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate
29m agoTrump's LA and San Diego comments 'dangerous, if not treasonous', say critics

blocks.text: Susan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate

blocks.caption: Robert Tait

blocks.text: Robert Tait

Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine, pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.

Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans, saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.

Collins’ defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.

Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.

Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.

“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Trump's LA and San Diego comments 'dangerous, if not treasonous', say critics
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump was accused of “dangerous, if not treasonous” behaviour after his comments suggesting he could “let [Iran] take out” Los Angeles or San Diego.
California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, has since directed the state’s emergency preparedness center to “actively monitor” possible threats to the state.

“Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs,” Newsom said in a post on X, adding that the state’s threat-assessment center would be on heightened alert “in the event that foreign actors interpret the president’s remarks as an invitation to target California”.

The president has faced a chorus of condemnation from Democratic leaders in California after his comments at a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, which the White House has suggested were being taken out of context.
At the president’s rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Trump claimed that high prices due to the war with Iran are a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”.
He went on:
double quotation markThey can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor vying to succeed Newsom, said he wasn’t surprised by the president’s comments.

“Donald Trump is a known commodity – you know how he acts, you know how he behaves,” Becerra told reporters at a campaign event in Los Angeles on Tuesday. But he took a jab at Republicans who “profess that they should be the leaders of our state” but aren’t willing to “stand up to Donald Trump”.
Meanwhile, San Diego mayor Todd Gloria said in a statement that “the most fundamental responsibility of a president is to protect the American people - all of them.”
He added:
double quotation markNo American city, regardless of its politics or geography, should ever be described as expendable or an acceptable price to pay.
But the White House insisted that Trump was being willfully misinterpreted.
Steven Cheung, its director of communications, posted on X:

double quotation markThe media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.
But one Republican House candidate, Jim Desmond, who is running in a competitive San Diego-based seat, pushed back.

“America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our commander in chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond, a former mayor of San Marcos, said in a statement.
In other developments:

items: The Cook Political Report has revised its predictions for the November midterm elections, saying “A Senate Majority is Squarely in Democrats’ Sights”. Cook amended its prediction for the Kansas Senate race from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up” – a shocker for a state where no Democrat has won a Senate election since 1932.

Donald Trump announced a massive new shipyard, which will be funded by a combination of federal and private dollars, at Tradepoint Atlantic in Sparrows Point. Anduril Industries, which is owned by Trump’s friend and donor Palmer Luckey, plans to invest $3.7bn in the shipyard and the US Navy will contribute an additional $2.9bn.

The USS Lincoln will dock in San Diego tomorrow, completing a nearly year-long deployment that sparked controversy over living conditions aboard the aircraft carrier as it supported military operations in Iran. Defense secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to greet the crew when they arrive.

Trump ordered the FBI to investigate protesters in Los Angeles who were demonstrating against the president’s immigration crackdown, according to a whistleblower complaint that was submitted to the Senate judiciary committee. Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, made the complaint following the federal response to anti-ICE demonstrations around the city’s federal buildings, and in residential area, early last year.

articles.title: How did Christa Pike survive execution attempt - and what happens next?
articles.summary: The convicted killer of Colleen Slemmer is said to be awake and speaking in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections.
articles.byline: James FitzGerald, Kayla Epstein, Brandon Drenon

blocks.text: Watch: What we know about Christa Pike’s "unprecedented" recovery after failed execution
ByJames FitzGeraldKayla Epstein and Brandon Drenon
Convicted murderer Christa Pike has woken up and begun speaking from her hospital bed almost a week after authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched her execution, her lawyers said.
Pike, 50, was sent to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her via lethal injection for the 1995 murder of a 19-year-old she met at a summer camp for troubled teens.
An independent review of what went wrong in the Nashville execution chamber on 30 September has been ordered by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee.
He has also halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing
How did Pike survive?
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.

Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, says it was not the case that Pike had some "special immunity" but suggested it was simply that not enough of the drug pentobarbital reached her bloodstream to kill her.
Pike was injected with a second dose of the drug, according to the prison authorities' protocol, after the first did not kill her.
In interviews with the BBC, Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream.
"Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating in her body, ended up in her arms, and that's how she lived," Zivot said.

Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition, was highlighted in advance by Pike's legal team as an additional issue that could scupper the process. Before the attempted execution, they had filed a legal case challenging the injection protocol.
If clots of blood formed at the injection site as a result of thrombocytosis, they would potentially have blocked the chemical from entering her veins, the lawyers warned.

As the attempted execution took place, prison officials used at least seven needles on Pike during their efforts to establish intravenous (IV) lines, Pike's lawyers said afterwards. The woman could simultaneously be heard "crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly".
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who was murdered by Pike and her then-boyfriend, told NBC the failed execution had been "a mess".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.

After it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the two doses, she was taken to hospital for life-saving treatment. States have a legal obligation not to deny medical treatment to prisoners.
What is pentobarbital?

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded".
But the department said the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective".
What happens next?
The full picture of Pike's current physical condition is unknown.

Although she was said to be awake and speaking in hospital as of 6 October, is it unclear whether she has any long-term health defects. Medical staff have been working to clear the drug from her body, a process that they expected to take about a week. She has been removed from a ventilator.
Zivot said Pike had been able to communicate in a "basic way", including by giving her name and making an incorrect attempt to guess the date.
Meanwhile she is reportedly handcuffed to her bed.
Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt
There is then the question of what happens to Pike next.

Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike, though executions in the state have been paused for the rest of the year. Meanwhile, it has been announced that the state's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada is stepping down.
Pike's lawyers have made repeated calls for Lee, the state governor, to commute her sentence to the lesser punishment of life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.

In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
The Supreme Court has already been involved in Pike's case: it allowed the lethal injections to go ahead after a legal battle.
Has this happened before?
While there is a lengthy history of botched executions across the US, Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived after receiving a lethal injection.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike is conscious and speaking.
There had been seven previous cases in which prisoners survived slated executions, but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.
What did Pike do? Who was Colleen Slemmer?
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder a year earlier of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, which was perpetrated along with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike killed Slemmer at a camp for troubled teens, after accusing Slemmer of insulting her and attempting to steal Shipp from her.
Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.

Shipp was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole and he remains in prison. He was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time.

Correction 1 October: This article originally referred to the inmate executed by the state of Louisiana in 1947 as Willie Smith. We have amended the article to make clear that his name was Willie Francis.

articles.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai
articles.summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in Chemistry

image.caption: The Norwegian Nobel Committee is responsible for selecting the Nobel Peace Prize laureatesImage: DW

blocks.text: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Last year, Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside. Their discoveries can help tackle some of the world's most pressing problems, like climate change.
What do laureates receive?

items: Laureates receive a tailored diploma, a medal and a document detailing the cash award that is set this year to 12 million Swedish kronor, which is equivalent to just over €1 million or $1.2 million.

blocks.text: Who else has received a Nobel Prize so far?

items: The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work on optogenetics, a method of controlling nerve cells with light, which makes it possible to study how the brain works.
The Nobel Prize in physics was awarded Tuesday to Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born astrophysicist whose efforts helped demistify a rare group of neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy.

blocks.text: Nobel prizes in literature and peace also this week

items: The Nobel Prize in literature is set to be awarded Thursday and the Nobel peace prize will be announced on Friday.
After that, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.
All prize announcements are streamed live by the Nobel Prize organization.
